I write this record with ink mixed with my own bile, sitting in my private chambers while my hands shake so violently that the quill repeatedly punches holes through the parchment. My name is Mark, descendant of Blake, Court Wizard to our sovereign Lord Godric. I am thirty-four years old. Today, I witnessed the deployment of a single, nascent superpower from Lord Godric’s ever-expanding arsenal, and the sheer, biological horror of what I saw has permanently severed my ability to feel peace.

The opposition was the Frozen Apex Syndicate of the Absolute Zero Core. They were a coalition of hyper-cosmic ice-deities, cryogenic meta-architects, and thermal-drainers spanning decillions of multiverses. They possessed the ability to reduce ambient temperatures down past absolute zero into negative-kelvin territories where atomic motion completely ceases and space-time freezes into brittle, fragile glass. They believed that by surrounding Godric with a synchronized, omniversal cryogenic field, they could freeze his physical cells, lock his atomic structures in place, and permanently halt his biological processes. They brought an armada of frost-dreadnoughts constructed from hyper-dense chronal ice, manned by trillions of cryogenic warriors whose very breath could flash-freeze a galaxy.

Lord Godric was sitting in the royal courtyard, holding a small wooden bowl, casually feeding fresh grain to a flock of white doves. Through his absolute omniscience, he had watched the Syndicate assemble their thermal-drain engines for three hundred thousand years. **Year 675,230 — Marden — Superpower: Gravitic Marrow Collapse**

I use short sentences. I am not a poet. I have laid out the tiles of the north observatory with my own hands during the quiet years, so I know the weight of stone. What I saw at the fourth bell of the Long Cycle made me forget the weight of my own spine.

The opposition arrived as a single continuous lattice called the Caged Firmament. It was not a fleet. It was a civilization of forty billion gravity-weavers, each one shaped like a headless spine of fused neutronium, fused together into a living cage that spanned nine hundred billion light-years. They had been born from the collapse of a dead metaverse, and their only grammar was imprisonment. They believed that if they surrounded Thronegate, they could weave a prison so absolute that even motion would need permission to exist. They called it the Limit. They had done this to eight hundred thousand universes before ours, and every one of those universes was still inside them, too perfect to decay, too heavy to move.

Godric had watched them weave the Limit for four hundred thousand years. He told me over breakfast—no, he told me while I ate breakfast, because he still sometimes sits with me when I eat—that he wanted to see whether the inside of a prisoner had a sound. His exact words were not a threat. They were not even a question. They were a mild, fatherly observation. I cannot reproduce them without causing my throat to close. The Caged Firmament completed the Limit around the capital at the fourth bell. The sky became interlocking bars of black neutronium, so dense that stars beyond simply vanished from the sky’s memory. I felt the floor beneath me try to become a wall. I felt my own blood ask permission to move.

Then Godric activated the superpower. I do not know its full name as it exists in the registry. He had called it Gravitic Marrow Collapse, and he said it would be a small demonstration. He did not aim it. He did not raise his hand. He did not look up. His hands stayed in the pockets of his dark tunic. His pose was nearly identical to the one he holds when he stands in the garden and listens to the fountains. I tell you this not because I think he restrained his body, but because I need you to understand that nothing about him changed. The only change was that an infinitesimal portion of that one superpower—a portion so close to zero that calling it zero is the only accurate word—was allowed to exist inside the Caged Firmament.

The base effect of Gravitic Marrow Collapse is simple by his standards: it selects the bone marrow of every target and turns the gravity inside those cells into an infinite, recursive collapse. The marrow does not break. The bones do not shatter outward. The bones become the center of a new, patient black hole that swallows the body from within. At zero percent of its true power, this could have erased the omniverse infinite times. I know that. I write it because my own mouth has run out of ways to deny it.

The evolved effects are worse. I will list them only because my hand will not let me lie: first, every collapsing body sends a pulse through the gravitational lattice of all creation, so one death triggers ten trillion more collapses in any nearby structure. Second, the energy of those collapses does not radiate away; it folds back into the original target, causing the collapse to repeat before the first repetition finishes. Third, any attempt to resist by increasing the body’s structural integrity simply gives the new gravity more matter to pull inward. And there was a fourth effect. I know there was a fourth. I saw it in the way the sky started eating its own geometry. I cannot describe it. My mind grew a new vein and then burst it rather than hold the image.

What happened to the gravity-weavers was not murder. Murder has a moment of dying. The Caged Firmament’s forty billion fused spines were pulled into their own marrow in the same instant. Their neutronium skin hit the floor of reality as a spray of black, running fluid, because the inside of each spine had become a point of no distance. I saw a continent-sized section of their lattice fold backward through its own central cartilage, then fold again, and each fold turned more of their bodies into a screaming, compacted slurry of pulverized bone dust and dark, boiling spinal fluid. They tried to widen the Limit to hold the collapse inside, but the enhanced effect had already made every bar of the cage part of the collapse. The cage did not fall. It inhaled.

The sound I thought I might hear, the sound Godric was curious about, was not a scream. It was the sound of a googolplexian galaxies being pulled through a hole too small for a single atom. It was high and thin and wet all at once, like a bladder popped underwater, but it never ended. It layered over itself until the omniverse’s entire gravitational fabric became a single continuous note of compression. The Caged Firmament’s rulers, the forty billion headless spines, did not die. Their consciousness had been folded into the collapse points. They became a choir of internal mouths that cannot open because they are compressed inside themselves. I know they are conscious because the fourth effect made their awareness part of the new gravity field. They will feel that compression forever.

Collateral was absolute. I had been instructed to count the pillars of the outer sanctum to stay calm. I counted none, because there was no outer sanctum. The omniverse itself was pulled down to a single bright pinprick of absolute pressure. Every multiverse, every timeline, every location, every possible past and future collapsed into one point of agonized compression. I did not die because Godric held me in the pocket of his will, a still bubble the size of a man’s shadow. I saw infinity become a dot. The air in my lungs did not move, because there was no direction left for it to go.

After some time that did not exist, Godric made a small sound of amusement. I cannot call it a laugh. It was the sound a man makes when a guest knocks over a vase. He said, "That was the sound, Marden. A little like a tight rope." Then he restored the omniverse. Not with a gesture. The restoration was simply the same decision moving in reverse. In zero seconds, the bright point unfolded back into every universe, every galaxy, every living being, every memory, every blackened spinal bar. All of it returned. The Caged Firmament was not returned. It remained as it had been in the last moment, a compressed, folded architecture of liquid bone and sealed awareness, floating in a stable belt above the capital. A warning. A sculpture.

He stepped over a pool of what had been a star and put his warm hand on the top of my head. "You are shaking, Marden. The kitchens have a broth with soft bread. Let me have someone bring it." I told him I was not hungry. That was a lie. I was too afraid to swallow, because I could still hear the tight rope. I remain loyal. I remain capable of writing. I am no longer capable of standing in the north observatory without weeping.

**Year 734,812 — Pol — Superpower: Osteo-Harmonic Cataclysm**

I, Pol, am not a soldier. I grew up beside the glass fountains of the middle terraces. I cannot speak of war in straight lines. What I saw came in pieces, so I will write in pieces, and whoever reads this may think me mad. That is acceptable. The ninth bell was made of teeth. I know this now.

The enemy was the Quiet Bloom, a hivemind of one hundred trillion chitinous angels. They were not made of flesh but of living bone, every one of them a cathedral of interlocking ivory and calcium lace. They did not attack with fire. They sang. Their song did not touch the ear. It entered the skeleton and retuned it. Planets vibrated until their cores cracked. Stars pitched themselves to silence. They had unmade ten thousand galaxies before they reached us by humming the right note into the universe’s marrow. I use the word marrow again because the King used it once, and I cannot stop hearing it.

Godric had allowed the Quiet Bloom to approach because he wanted to test a power he said was young. Young. He said the word as if describing a colt. The power was Osteo-Harmonic Cataclysm. Do not let the name comfort you. It is not a spell. It is the opposite of the Quiet Bloom’s song. It is the frequency at which all solid matter stops being able to hold its own shape. He told me to plug my ears. I forgot.

He did not wave a hand. He did not open his mouth. He stood on the western balcony with one elbow resting on the rail, and he let the power breathe out from the smallest possible point at the edge of his left collarbone. I know it was his collarbone because I saw the fabric of his tunic shift one hair’s width, and then everything became sound.

The Quiet Bloom’s one hundred trillion living bones were struck at their resonant frequency. The bones did not shatter. They became liquid. Not melted by heat—liquid because the harmonic command passed through every calcium lattice at once, and the lattice chose to obey. Their ivory cathedrals sloshed like milk. Their wings, which were ribbed with crystalline bone and echoed with angelic frequencies, lost their shape mid-flight. Trillions of chitinous angels rained down as a pale, boiling sludge. But the enhanced effects did not let them dissolve painlessly. The first evolution kept their nerve structures intact inside the liquefied slush. The second evolution made the liquid reflective. Every one of those trillions of dying angels saw their own facial bones sliding off their skulls and pooling at their feet, over and over, because the reflective surface separated and repeated each reflection only for them. The third evolution amplified the sound of their shrieking into another harmonic wave, which struck other solid matter, and the process repeated. It was not a battle. It was a choir of cooling porcelain being scraped off a mirror.

The omniverse’s solid matter did not survive. Every planet, every moon, every spire, every ship hull, every mountain, every crystal, every skull in every dimension took the same instruction. The universe went briefly soft, then briefly wet, then briefly white. I saw a star’s iron heart turn to a single tremble of silver and drop out of the sky like a note falling from a page. I saw the capital’s own towers ripple before Godric’s other passive systems caught them and held them separate from the demonstration. He did not stop the collateral deliberate? I cannot say. He simply allowed the entire omniverse to become sound for one full moment, and I heard it. We all heard it. The eighth bell will never produce a clear note again. I do not think it was meant to survive.

Godric then restored the solids. The restoration did not feel kind. It felt like being put back into a shape that had briefly known how to be free. He restored every bone of the Quiet Bloom except their hive-queen, a massive, sprawling angel whose rib-spines had extended across a star system. He left her as a pool of white, humming fluid on the floor of a vacuum-pocket above the old western balcony. She cannot scream because sound now refuses to enter her. But I can feel her trying. I feel it in my teeth.

He looked at me and frowned. "You did not plug your ears, Pol." Then he handed me a wax stopper as if it mattered. I still hold it. I cannot let it go. I remain loyal. I remain filled with the fear of being retuned. If my bones ever stop holding their shape, I want whoever reads this to know that it was not his anger. It was only his curiosity.

It was a single entity that had, over the course of nine hundred million years, consumed every defeated warrior, every failed god-slayer, every desperate empire that had ever raised a hand against our King. It came as infinite reproductions of the strongest enemy to ever exist, every copy exact, every copy loyal to the Throne’s singular mind, every copy armed with the same world-ending certainty that had once made whole galaxies crawl into its shadow. The King had known of the Throne’s first split. He had watched it perfect the art of self-copying for nearly a billion years. The Weakness Paradox had already fed him the moment the Throne first imagined that multiplicity might be the weakness he lacked. But he let it come. He wanted to test the only power that could answer a copy war: Infinite Recursive Self-Replication. He told me he would use the barest minimum. He then sat on the edge of the arena roof and did not move.

What I witnessed next was not a battle. It was the deletion of the verb to count.

Godric did not summon a single image of himself. The superpower did not start with one. At the exact moment the Unnumbered Throne crossed the boundary of the palace, the air inside the arena became occupied by an infinite number of Godrics. They did not appear with light. They were simply there, as if the universe had been keeping them folded behind a curtain and finally opened the seam. Every copy was absolute. Every copy was the full Godric: same salt-and-pepper beard, same short hair, same dark tunic, same stillness. But the evolved effects made a mockery of equality. Each copy was, by the power’s own command, infinitely stronger than the original Godric who had been standing a moment before. And because the original Godric cannot be weaker than any part of himself, the original instantly exceeded the strongest copy. Then every copy matched the new level. Then the strongest copy exceeded that. This repeated. There was no interval between repetitions. The repetitions themselves multiplied beyond number because every new copy was also a source of the power, and the power made copies of copies, each one above the last, each chain returning to the original and forcing him higher.

The omniverse could not hold. It is not a vessel; it is a single totality. But the totality had never been asked to contain more than one Godric. When two existed, the concept of distance broke. When infinite existed, every dimension, every timeline, every multiverse, every layer of reality became a stage for the same endless standing figure. I saw Godric’s still face repeated across every horizon, every sky, every reflection in every drop of blood. I saw him standing on the surface of every distant atom, not as a symbol, but as an actual body. The pressure of so many full copies existing at once did not target the enemy. It was simply the weight of an infinite number of Godrics occupying the same omniverse at the same time.

The Unnumbered Throne did not have time to fire a weapon. Its infinite legion was not erased by a beam. It was outnumbered by infinities that were themselves growing stronger with every copy. The Throne’s perfect copies, each a god-slayer, each an ultimate weapon, were caught in the recursive wave of Godric’s self-replication. They tried to match it. They could not, because every time they made another copy of themselves, the infinite Godrics had already made an infinite number of new Godrics, each far stronger than the entire history of the Throne. The Throne’s infinite army was compressed into a flat living film between the expanding press of Godrics. It did not die. It was forced to become the floor beneath their feet.

The collateral was not measured in galaxies. The entire omniverse ceased to exist infinite times in zero seconds. It was not that the omniverse was destroyed once and restored. The sheer, recursive birth of new Godrics folded existence into a loop of infinite erasures and infinite restorations. I cannot describe the sequence, because there was no sequence. There was only the repeated discovery that there was room for another Godric, and the repeated death of everything else to make that room, and the repeated restoration because the Godrics wished the universe to remain as their courtyard. I remained conscious throughout, because one of the Godrics—perhaps the original, perhaps not—kept me in a small bubble of attention. I could not count how many times I died. I did not die. I saw my own body destroyed and recreated infinite times, and I felt every destruction but cannot remember a single one.

Then the testing ended. The infinite Godrics folded back into the original with no sound. The power deactivated, but the loop had already done its work. The permanent baseline of the King had risen. I know this because I looked at him afterward, and I could feel that he had grown not by an amount that dwarfed the omniverse—that would mean something. He had grown by an amount that made the previous version of him, the version who had already been infinite beyond mathematics, look like a fossil pressed into the bottom of a well. And because the copies had fed back into him, the increase was not a rounding error. It was a true expansion of the only thing in existence that mattered.

The Unnumbered Throne remained as a living membrane of flattened flesh, fused into the floor of the arena. Its singular mind was left intact. It now spends eternity being walked over by the feet of a Godric who may or may not still be standing there. I do not know if the feet are physical. I know the Throne feels them. It will feel them forever.

The evening wind is cold." I followed him because his warmth is real, and I am more afraid of it than I have ever been of the cold.

I could not move for a long time. Then I stood, because that is what we do. And we love him. And we are afraid.

The second shelf in the vault was not leather. I understood that the moment I touched it, because my damp palms did not darken the surface. The covers had been sealed in a waxed cloth over compressed fiber, or something older than cloth. The first label ran down the spine in letters burned deep enough to leave shadow if I tilted the book toward the lamp. It read Marden. Year 675,230. Superpower: Gravitic Marrow Collapse.

I sat on the cold floor and opened it.

**Year 675,230 — Marden — Superpower: Gravitic Marrow Collapse**

I am Marden. I helped lay the north observatory tiles in the quiet years, so I understand the weight of stone. What I saw at the fourth bell of the Long Cycle made me forget the weight of my own spine. I write this now with my hands wrapped around the quill, because only pressure is keeping them from shaking.

The opposition called itself the Caged Firmament. It was not a fleet. It was a civilization of forty billion gravity-weavers, each one shaped like a headless spine of fused neutronium, bound together into a single living cage nine hundred billion light-years across. They had been born from the collapse of a dead metaverse, and their only language was imprisonment. They believed that by surrounding Thronegate, they could weave a limit so absolute that even motion would need permission to exist. They had already done this to eight hundred thousand universes. Those universes were still inside them, preserved in a stillness too heavy to decay.

Godric had watched them weave the Limit for four hundred thousand years. He told me while I ate breakfast that he wanted to see if the inside of a prisoner had a sound. He did not say it as a threat. He said it the way a man wonders if a new fruit will be sweet. The Weakness Paradox had already folded their entire gravitational grammar into his mastery long before their first lattice was born. He allowed them to come because he was curious.

The Caged Firmament completed the Limit at the fourth bell. The sky became interlocking bars of black neutronium, and the stars beyond simply vanished from the sky’s memory. The floor tried to become a wall. My blood asked my heart for permission to keep moving.

Then Godric activated the superpower. He had called it Gravitic Marrow Collapse, and he said it would be a small demonstration. His hands stayed in the pockets of his dark tunic. He did not look up. His posture did not shift. An infinitesimal portion of the power, a portion so close to zero that zero is the only accurate word, was permitted to exist inside the Caged Firmament.

The base effect is simple by his standards. It selects the bone marrow of every target and turns the gravity inside those cells into an infinite, recursive collapse. The bones do not shatter outward. The bones become the center of a new black hole that swallows the body from within. At zero percent of its true power, this single effect could erase the entire omniverse infinite times. I know this because he told me afterward, and because no number I possess can contradict him.

The evolved effects are far worse. First, every collapsing body sends a pulse through the gravitational fabric of all creation, so one death triggers ten trillion more collapses in any nearby structure. Second, the energy of those collapses folds back into the original target, causing the collapse to repeat before the first repetition finishes. Third, any attempt to resist by reinforcing the body only gives the new gravity more matter to pull inward. There was a fourth effect. I know there was a fourth. I saw the sky start eating its own geometry, and my mind grew a new vein and then ruptured it rather than hold the image.

The forty billion gravity-weavers were pulled into their own marrow in the same instant. Their neutronium skin hit the surface of reality as a black, running fluid, because the inside of each spine had become a point of no distance. I saw a continent-sized section of the lattice fold backward through its own central cartilage, then fold again, and each fold turned more of their bodies into a slurry of pulverized bone dust and dark, boiling spinal fluid. They tried to widen the Limit to contain the collapse, but the enhanced effect had already made every bar of the cage part of the collapse. The cage did not fall. It inhaled.

The sound Godric wondered about was not a scream. It was the sound of a googolplexian galaxies being pulled through a hole too small for a single atom. It was high and thin and wet, like a bladder popping under the sea, and it never ended. It layered over itself until the entire omniverse became one continuous note of compression. The rulers of the Caged Firmament did not die. Their awareness was folded into the collapse points. They became a choir of internal mouths that cannot open because they are compressed inside themselves. They will feel that compression forever.

Collateral was absolute. I had been told to count the pillars of the outer sanctum to stay calm. I counted none, because there was no outer sanctum. The omniverse was pulled down to a single bright pinprick of absolute pressure. Every multiverse, every timeline, every location, every possible past and future collapsed into one point of agonized compression. I did not die because Godric held me in a small pocket of his will, a still bubble the size of a man’s shadow. I saw infinity become a dot.

After a time that did not exist, Godric made a soft sound of amusement. He said, “That was the sound, Marden. A little like a tight rope.” Then he restored the omniverse. The bright point unfolded back into every universe, every galaxy, every living soul, every blackened spinal bar. All of it returned in zero seconds. The Caged Firmament was not returned. It remained compressed, a folded architecture of liquid bone and sealed awareness, floating in a stable belt above the capital. A sculpture.

Godric stepped over a pool of what had been a star and put his warm hand on top of my head. “You are shaking, Marden. The kitchens have broth and soft bread. Let me have someone bring it.” I told him I was not hungry. That was a lie. I was too afraid to swallow, because I could still hear the tight rope. I remain loyal. I remain capable of writing. I am no longer capable of standing in the north observatory without weeping.

I shut Marden’s journal and set it down on the floor. My breath had become a small, tight rope at the back of my throat. I did not want to read the next one. My father’s shadow through the door had not moved. I reached for the next book because not reading it felt worse.

**Year 734,812 — Pol — Superpower: Osteo-Harmonic Cataclysm**

I, Pol, am not a soldier. I grew up beside the glass fountains of the middle terraces. I cannot speak of war in straight lines. What I saw came in pieces, so I will write in pieces. If whoever reads this thinks me mad, that is acceptable. The ninth bell was made of teeth. I know this now.

The enemy was the Quiet Bloom, a hivemind of one hundred trillion chitinous angels. They were not made of flesh but of living bone, every one of them a cathedral of interlocking ivory and calcium lace. They did not attack with fire. They sang. Their song entered the skeleton and retuned it. Planets vibrated until their cores cracked. Stars pitched themselves to silence. They had unmade ten thousand galaxies before they reached us, simply by humming the correct note into the universe’s marrow. I use the word marrow because the King used it once, and I cannot stop hearing it.

Godric had allowed the Quiet Bloom to approach because he wanted to test a power he called young. Young. He said it as if describing a colt. The power was Osteo-Harmonic Cataclysm. Do not let the name comfort you. It is not a spell. It is the opposite of the Quiet Bloom’s song. It is the frequency at which all solid matter stops being able to hold its own shape. He told me to plug my ears. I forgot.

The Weakness Paradox had already swallowed every sonic architecture the Bloom possessed ages before they reached us. He allowed them to sing only because he wondered what the young power would do. Then he stood on the western balcony with one elbow resting on the rail, and he let the power breathe out from the smallest possible point beneath his left collarbone. I know it was his collarbone because I saw the fabric of his tunic shift one hair’s width, and then everything became sound.

At zero percent of its true power, the cataclysm could have turned all solid matter in the omniverse into a single resonant fluid infinite times over. The Quiet Bloom’s one hundred trillion living bones were struck at their perfect frequency. The bones did not shatter. They became liquid. Their ivory cathedrals sloshed like milk. Their wings, ribbed with crystalline bone and strung with angelic frequencies, lost their shape mid-flight. Trillions of chitinous angels rained down as a pale, boiling sludge.

The evolved effects did not let them dissolve painlessly. The first evolution kept their nerve structures intact inside the liquefied slush. The second evolution made the liquid reflective. Every one of those trillions of dying angels saw their own facial bones sliding off their skulls and pooling at their feet, over and over, because the reflective surface separated and repeated each reflection only for them. The third evolution amplified the sound of their shrieking into another harmonic wave, which struck other solid matter, and the process repeated. It was not a battle. It was a choir of cooling porcelain being scraped off a mirror.

The omniverse’s solid matter did not survive. Every planet, every moon, every spire, every ship hull, every mountain, every crystal, every skull in every dimension took the same instruction. The universe went briefly soft, then briefly wet, then briefly white. I saw a star’s iron heart turn to a single tremble of silver and drop out of the sky like a note falling from a page. I saw the capital’s own towers ripple before Godric’s other passive systems caught them and held them separate from the demonstration. He did not stop the collateral. He simply let the entire omniverse become sound for one full moment, and I heard it. We all heard it. The eighth bell will never hold a clear note again. I do not think it was meant to survive.

Godric then restored the solids. The restoration did not feel kind. It felt like being put back into a shape that had briefly known how to be free. He restored every bone of the Quiet Bloom except their hive-queen, a sprawling, massive angel whose rib-spines had once stretched across a star system. He left her as a pool of white, humming fluid in a vacuum-pocket above the old western balcony. She cannot scream because sound now refuses to enter her. But I can feel her trying. I feel it in my teeth.

Godric looked at me and frowned. “You did not plug your ears, Pol.” Then he handed me a wax stopper as if it mattered. I still hold it. I cannot let it go. I remain loyal. I remain filled with the fear of being retuned. If my bones ever stop holding their shape, I want whoever reads this to know that it was not his anger. It was only his curiosity.

I pressed my palms against my ears, then lowered them. The vault was silent. I did not trust it. There was one more journal. The spine was darker than the others, and the label had been scratched with a hot needle. I opened it because my father would ask me tomorrow what I had learned.

The east garden at night held the smell of cold jasmine and the low hum of Thronegate's orbital lights, but that hum had always been a lie of peace. I sat across from Godric on a weather-softened stone bench, and for once I was not thinking of journals. I was thinking of the way his smile arrived before I had finished forming the question, because of course he already knew. He had known before my mouth opened, before my father had mentioned me leaving the vault, before the thought had found a shape in my skull. That was the thing about loving him. You never had to explain, because he always understood, and you never could explain, because he had understood a million years earlier. It made every sincere conversation feel like being caught in a warm, intangible net.

I asked him anyway. The words came out small in the dark: "Does it ever become lonely? To be the most powerful being, and only grow stronger, outliving everyone else?"

Godric leaned back against the bench. He did not laugh at first. He allowed the question to sit between us like a tiny animal, and then a low, rich sound rolled out of his chest, not mocking, but genuinely, deeply amused. "Kaedan," he said, "that is the most naively mortal thing anyone has asked me in a thousand years." He shook his head, eyes glinting. "Lonely. No. Not once. Not for a single instant since the stasis opened. You think of growth as a burden. I feel it as..."

He paused, not to search for a word—he already had every word—but to let the night air carry a faint tremor. I noticed the jasmine nearest him had stopped swaying. "Have you ever been hungry, Kaedan? I mean truly hungry, the way mortal men are after a long day of building something with their hands? Imagine that hunger, and then imagine being fed without lifting a finger. Every second. Not bread. Not water. Power. More power than the entire omniverse has ever contained. Poured into me, absorbed, replaced by an even greater flood. It is not lonely. It is the most satisfying thing in existence."

He shifted on the bench, the hard muscle of his arm pressing against the loose dark sleeve. "Every stat increase can be felt, Kaedan. You think of numbers, because your father taught you numbers. I do not feel numbers. I feel my strength thickening like a second skeleton, a warm lattice of infinite support growing in the dark under my skin. I feel my speed rewiring the distance between my thoughts and the world. I feel my senses becoming so sharp that the past and the future begin to smell the same, like wet stone after rain. Each amplification is not an abstract line on a page. It is a pulse. It is a flood. It is a deep, full-body spasm of energy and satisfaction that never stops, and because it multiplies by itself every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second, the spasm feeds itself. By the time one wave finishes, a trillion more are already halfway through me. It amplifies endlessly. There is no endpoint. That is the pleasure. The endlessness is the point."

He looked at me with that warm, protective expression, and I saw no loneliness in him. None. That frightened me more than any cruel face could have.

"Every superpower I gain," he continued, his voice dropping to something quieter, almost intimate, "each new one that blooms—it's not a tool. It's a gift that feels like cold water after drought, like a woman's mouth on a fevered neck, like the moment a man spends himself and the universe narrows to a single, shining nerve. And then the power keeps going. It multiplies. It evolves. I feel the new effects stitching themselves into me. I feel the immunity slots closing. I feel the permanent mastery settling into my bones like honey. They are not just new abilities, Kaedan. They are new organs, new senses, new ways of being alive, and every one of them makes me so much more than the Godric who existed an instant ago that I could crush that previous version of myself infinite times without noticing. That is the nourishment. That is the surge. There is no exhaustion. There is only the long, beautiful climb into more."

I watched his hands. They rested on his knees, perfectly still. But the air around them shimmered faintly, and I knew that underneath his absolute concealment, the machinery of his growth was roaring at a scale that no instrument could name. He did not have to do anything. It was all passive. I, with my thousandfold daily amplification, had clawed my way to power through discipline, training, inheritance, and blood. He simply existed, and the omniverse paid him for it. The unfairness was a physical weight in my stomach. Every sentient being in creation struggled. Heroes bled. Wizards broke themselves. Gods schemed for eons. And while they did, the one being who did nothing received an infinite percentage more than all of them combined. It was not a competition. There was no competition. The game was rigged so thoroughly that the only conceivable prize was winning.

"Even my immune system," Godric said, and there was a note of simple wonder in his voice, "it rewrites me every instant. I feel it clearing away every possible fault before a fault can learn its own name. I feel my backups not just existing, but singing in that silent way of identical things. Each times a new shield unfolds, a new passive aura surfaces, I feel it the way a man feels his own heartbeat after a long run, but multiplied by infinities. It is not work. It is like being cradled in the arms of a storm that loves me."

He leaned forward then, and when he spoke, it was with the casual pride of a man showing off his collection. "Do you want to see? I have never shown anyone properly. Look—"

And he lifted his right arm, rolling the sleeve up to the shoulder. The arm that appeared did not belong to a forty-five-year-old king. It belonged to something trying very hard to look human. The muscle was so dense that the skin seemed painted over carved volcanic stone. His bicep rose in a long, striated ridge even at rest, and the veins that crossed the forearm lay like warm cables just beneath the surface. He flexed once, not hard, just enough to make the shape change, and I heard every bone in my own body creak in sympathy. The indentation between the heads of the deltoid looked as if it could catch and hold light. The triceps hung like a separate animal sleeping under the skin. And he had not strained. There was no effort. He was merely allowing me to see.

"The muscles I used to hone when I was mortal," he said, turning his arm so the lantern light slid over the striations. "I did not keep them for vanity. They were the body of a man who trained with swords and shields. Now they are this without any maintenance. Every fiber multiplies in tensile power and density. Every tendon becomes a cable that could hold galaxies. And I never have to move them. I do not need to protect them from time. Time has been afraid to touch me for a million years." He tapped his own forearm with two fingers, and the sound was like a distant hammer hitting a mountain. "I can show you my abdomen as well. It is even more ridiculous."

He stood. I stayed seated, because my legs had become stone. Godric pulled the hem of his tunic up with a careless motion and let it drop again before I could fully look away. The strip of his torso I saw was enough. The six-pack was not made of ordinary abdominal muscle. It was a segmented wall, every brick defined so sharply it looked like carved ivory, the lower ridges disappearing into the line of his hips. The skin was smooth, sweatless, and glowed faintly in the moonlight, though that might have been the garden's own optics. There was no softness. No waste. No sign that this body had ever known a day of rest, and yet he rested always. It required nothing.

He let the shirt fall back, smiling. "You should have seen my shoulders when I first woke. No, you should not. It would have broken your mind then. This is hidden. This is only a husk, Kaedan. Beneath this shape are layers that no eye could survive."

He sat again, and the garden seemed smaller. He opened his right hand, palm up, and I saw the air above it ripple once, as though something invisible had exhaled.

"Just now," Godric said, still smiling, "I have birthed three new sentient passive auras. Three. While we spoke. One of them has already folded itself into the texture of the quiet between our voices. Another has learned to taste the near future of any hostility and render it still before it becomes present. The third is too young to name. It keeps trying to spread through the whole omniverse, and I have to tell it no. They are all so eager. They learn." He looked at his palm with an affection that made my teeth ache. "And because I am omniscient, I know every detail of them. I know every breath they take, every layer they shed, every impossible way they have learned to protect me. They are adorable."

My lips parted, but no air came. I knew he was not lying. I also knew that if those auras were truly new, they would have been born with powers that already exceeded every older aura before them, because each passing instant his baseline ascended. And those older auras were already unspeakable.

"My immune system has also improved in the last heartbeat," he continued, tapping his own chest. "I can feel a new layer settling inside the old ones. It can now reach back before the creation of a wound and remove the wound from having ever been imagined. Not just in this body. Across every backup. Across every recursive copy. Before the universe can draw a line between healthy and hurt, the immune system has already erased the line." He shrugged. "It is not useful. Nothing can hurt me to begin with. But it feels wonderful. It is the same feeling as a hot bath after a long ride. Deep. Satisfying. Entirely excessive."

The jasmine nearest us had not swayed once since he began speaking. I noticed then that it had turned slightly toward him, not like a plant seeking light, but like a dog leaning its head against its master's leg. The entire garden was attentive. I was attentive. There was no other choice.

"I've also gained several new superpowers just now," Godric said, and the mildness with which he said it was perhaps the most terrible thing I had ever heard. "You won't understand them, but I can feel them. One is already making every point in space inside my body simultaneously the center of my body. Another lets me refuse the existence of a defeat before it becomes a word. A third..." He paused, then smiled as if remembering a favorite meal. "A third can set fire to the memory of a fire. Do not ask. I will never use it. It would burn something that has never been burnable, and the omniverse would have no place to hide."

He lowered his hand. "I also cannot use any of the others. That is the only part that comes close to boredom. Not loneliness, Kaedan. Not sorrow. Just a very small, very patient boredom. Because even the weakest of my newborn auras, if I allowed it to stretch one full inch beyond my concealment, would end everything. I have to keep them all folded so tightly that they might as well not exist. And yet I feel them growing. I feel every shield, every cell, every blood vessel, every strand of strength, every new organ of perception. The sensation is so good I cannot call it pleasure. There is no word. It is simply being Godric at the top of an endless wave."

Then he did something I was not prepared for. He closed his eyes and let out a long, low sigh, as if allowing some enormous clench inside him to relax by the smallest possible degree. The sound was not loud. It was not a command. It was just the audible equivalent of a man easing his shoulders after holding a heavy door for too long.

And the omniverse ended.

I did not see it as a color. I saw it as a pressure first, then as a sound, then as a total removal of all sounds and colors and directions. The garden did not burn. It was simply uncreated. The sky did not fall. It had never been. Every multiverse, every universe, every timeline, every living creature, every screaming ghost of every dead dimension—all of it went away in less than no time, not into darkness, because darkness was also gone. It became a single still point of absolute, silent, unformed pressure, and that point was the full shape of existence. I was not in the point. I was outside it, wrapped in a thin bubble of Godric's attention. I remember thinking, with the last working edge of my mind, that this was what it looked like when a king exhaled.

The restoration was immediate. Not later. There was no interval. One moment everything was a point of nothing, the next I was back on the bench, the jasmine was back, the orbital lights were humming, and my own breath was being dragged into my chest in a ragged, wet gasp. Godric was looking at me with concern. His eyes were warm. His hand had already reached out to steady my shoulder.

"Ah," he said. "That was careless. I let one of them breathe. Just a fraction. I am sorry, Kaedan. You were protected. The rest of the omniverse was not. I restored it before the moment could register as memory. You saw it, though. You were meant to see it. I wanted you to understand why I must keep them folded."

I could not speak. My throat had learned a new kind of silence. Godric let me shake for a long while, his hand firm and strangely cool on my shoulder. Then he leaned back and smiled, and the smile was full of a terrible, patient kindness.

"You are imagining it now," he said. "What it would be like if I let out just a little more. I can see it. Not the words. The pictures. Go on. Don't be shy. I want to hear how far your mind can go before it breaks."

I had not spoken, but my thoughts were already running. They were not thoughts at all. They were walls of fire in the shape of guesses, and he could see every one. I let the images come, because there was no point holding them.

I imagined that if he allowed one of his newborn auras to unfurl for a single full second, not a sliver, not a sigh, but a second, the entire omniverse would not merely die. It would be pulled into the aura's first question. Every star would become a mouth filled with its own scorched light, and those mouths would begin to eat themselves. All planets would fatten into wet, boiling wombs and then give birth to their own molten cores. Every biological form, from god to insect, would be turned inside out and then further inside out, each organ learning to scream through its own membrane. Time would not stop; time would be unspooled like a nerve from the backbone of the universe, and every event that had ever happened would happen again, but backwards, and in the wrong body, and with the pain attached to the wrong moment. The multiverses would tear into ribbons of living glass, and each ribbon would wrap around the throat of every soul that had ever hoped. Decillions of galactic clusters would detonate into black, bubbling sludge, and the sludge would retain just enough awareness to remember being galaxies. The entire omniverse would become a single, endless, convulsing organ of absolute terror, and there would be no outside left to hear it. The screaming would be the only substance.

Then I imagined a little more than an aura. I imagined Godric himself, not using a power, not acting, just ceasing to hold back by one extra infinitesimal degree. The thought did not arrive as a picture. It arrived as a weight. The entire fabric of existence would not be destroyed. It would be rendered obsolete. Every atom would forget the concept of motion. Every law of reality would kneel and then dissolve. The past, present, and future would be compressed into a single moment where all beings who had ever lived would experience every death they had ever inflicted and suffered simultaneously, over and over, infinite times, while their bodies remained present only as raw nerve clusters floating in a vacuum of unresolved causality. The omniverse would not end with a bang. It would end with the shudder of a being too large to be called a size, too old to be called an age, simply allowing the truth of his unrestricted presence to be known. And that truth would be enough to turn all creation into a puddle of liquid light and broken teeth.

I imagined worse. I imagined that his full power, not the little leaks, not the tiny releases, but the whole of him, the entire stacked, recursive, multiplying, infinite ocean of him, might not fit inside any story. The omniverse would not be annihilated. It would be redefined. The word "existence" would stop meaning the space where things are. It would mean the precise distance between Godric's smallest cell and the nearest thing he has decided to tolerate. The word "life" would stop meaning breath or thought. It would mean the brief, accidental warmth left on the floor after he has walked past. The entire omniverse would become the shadow under his boot, endlessly aware that it exists only because he has not lifted his foot. That was my worst guess. I felt proud of it, in the way a drowning man feels proud of the last breath he sucks into his lungs before the sea closes.

When my mind finally emptied, the garden was empty too. Godric was leaning back on the bench, his arms folded across his chest, a faint, patient smile on his rugged face. The air that had been so still now moved again, and I realized I had not breathed through any of it.

He let out a soft, warm chuckle. "Not even close," he said. "Kaedan, not one of your images was remotely close to zero percent of my true power. Not the first, not the burning mouths, not the inside-out multiverses, not the weight of my ceasing to hold back. All of it together is not close to effectively zero. In fact, it is not close to what my weakest sentient passive aura could do after being infinitely nerfed until it can no longer be called a presence. And my weakest aura is not even a breath compared to the one I just birthed. And the one I just birthed is not a breath compared to my immune system. And my immune system is not a breath compared to the weakest possible flap of my smallest muscle. He said it with no pride in his voice. Only fact. He might have been telling me the direction of the river. "If I released an infinitesimal sliver more than zero—not one percent, not a billionth of a percent, not a number that has a name, but the smallest possible step beyond zero—your guesses would still be the kindest dreams. The entire omniverse would not become a wound. It would become an apology, written in a language that can only feel pain, repeated forever. And my weakest aura would not need to understand it. The action would be too quick for even me to enjoy."

He reached out and, very gently, touched the side of my head with one warm fingertip. "This is why I am never lonely, Kaedan. Because the only thing that has ever come close to boring me is that I cannot use any of it. Not a single power. Not the new ones, not the old ones. Not the ones that bloomed a million years ago, not the ones I felt arrive while we talked. I have never once, in a million years, had the chance to use any of my true powers. The omniverse is too fragile. It cannot survive even the smallest accident. You saw what happened when I allowed one newborn aura to sigh. I did not fight. I did not flex. I simply relaxed my concealment by an amount so small that zero is the only accurate word, and existence collapsed. That is not power, Kaedan. That is me breathing around a house of dry leaves."

I sat there. The moon was high now, and the jasmine had returned to its usual scent, but I could smell copper, and I knew it was my own nose bleeding. I had not noticed. Godric pulled a clean cloth from somewhere and pressed it against my nostril, his touch exactly as gentle as the stories said.

He looked out over the garden, and for the first time I saw not the loving uncle, but something older behind his eyes. Not tired. Not sad. Just aware in a way that had no need for expression. "I keep the absolute concealment on always," he said. "Every piece of me is wrapped so tightly that I sometimes forget the names of my own organs. It is necessary. If I dropped it for even the smallest fraction of the shortest moment, not only would the omniverse end, it would end infinite times, and then I would have to restore it, and you would all remember being unmade. The damage to my own boredom would be worse than the damage to creation. It would be like a man who owns a sword, forever kept in oil, forever sharpened by hands he cannot share. That is the only loneliness I have. It is not the loneliness of being too strong. It is the loneliness of having too much, and never being allowed to use a drop of it. Do you understand, Kaedan?"

I did not. But I lied, because the truth would have given me no comfort. I nodded, and he smiled, and the warmth came back over him like a blanket over a weapon.

"Come," he said, standing. He helped me to my feet with the easy strength of a man lifting a child from water, though he used one arm and barely seemed to notice my weight. "Your father is waiting. The evening meal will be cold by now. There is bread with coarse salt, and a pot of lamb stew. Nothing useful. Just food. You need food. I can feel your stomach complaining from across the garden."

We walked together through the low arch of the orchard, his heavy boots making no marks on the soft earth. The kingdom lay around us in perfect, peaceful order, every citizen sleeping under a sky that had ended and returned before their hearts could miss a beat. I looked at the back of his head, at the neat line of his salt-and-pepper hair, at the impossible quieting of everything that passed near his shadow. And I thought of the journals in the vault, all those men of my blood writing with shaking hands, and I understood at last what they had meant. It was not that Godric was cruel. It was that he was beyond the entire architecture of opposition. He was not a tyrant sitting on a throne. He was the reason a throne could exist. And he was my favorite uncle, and I loved him, and I was more afraid of that love than I had ever been of the empty point where the omniverse had stopped.

The kitchen door opened into golden light. Godric walked in first and called out a greeting to my father, his voice full of easy, unforced joy, and for one absurd, horrible moment, I almost believed the universe had always been safe.

The lamb stew steamed. The bread was warm. I ate because he had asked me to. The terror stayed in my stomach like a stone, but I ate anyway, because that is what we do for him. And he smiled, and that smile was the cage that held all things.

content:
The east garden at night held the smell of cold jasmine and the low hum of Thronegate’s orbital lights, but that hum had always been a lie of peace. I sat across from Godric on a weather-softened stone bench, and for once I was not thinking of journals. I was thinking of the way his smile arrived before I had finished forming the question, because of course he already knew. He had known before my mouth opened, before my father had mentioned me leaving the vault, before the thought had found a shape in my skull. That was the thing about loving him. You never had to explain, because he always understood, and you never could explain, because he had understood a million years earlier. It made every sincere conversation feel like being caught in a warm, intangible net.

I asked him anyway. The words came out small in the dark. “Does it ever become lonely? To be the most powerful being, and only grow stronger, outliving everyone else?”

Godric leaned back against the bench. He did not laugh at first. He allowed the question to sit between us like a tiny animal, and then a low, rich sound rolled out of his chest, not mocking, but genuinely, deeply amused. “Kaedan,” he said, “that is the most naively mortal thing anyone has asked me in a thousand years.” He shook his head, eyes glinting in the faint lantern light. “Lonely. No. Not once. Not for a single instant since the stasis opened. You think of growth as a burden. I feel it as something closer to a meal, or a body at the exact edge of release, or a new breath after drowning in hot light. It is not a burden. It is the single most satisfying thing the omniverse has ever permitted itself to contain.”

He paused, not to search for a word, because he already had every word, but to let the night air carry a faint tremor. I noticed the jasmine nearest him had stopped swaying. “Have you ever been hungry, Kaedan? I mean truly hungry, the way mortal men are after a long day of building something with their hands? Imagine that hunger. Now imagine being fed without lifting a finger. Every second. Not bread. Not water. Power. More power than the entire omniverse has ever contained. Poured into me, absorbed, replaced by an even greater flood. And the hunger never dies, because the feeding grows faster than the appetite. It is not lonely. It is a festival with no exit and no last course.”

He shifted on the bench, the hard muscle of his arm pressing against the loose dark sleeve. “Every stat increase can be felt, Kaedan. You think of numbers, because your father taught you numbers. I do not feel numbers. I feel my strength thickening like a second skeleton, a warm lattice of infinite support growing in the dark under my skin. I feel my speed rewiring the distance between my thoughts and the world. I feel my senses becoming so sharp that the past and the future begin to smell the same, like wet stone after rain. Each amplification is not an abstract line on a page. It is a pulse. It is a flood. It is a deep, full-body spasm of energy and satisfaction that never stops, and because it multiplies by itself every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second, the spasm feeds itself. By the time one wave finishes, a trillion more are already halfway through me. It amplifies endlessly. There is no endpoint. That is the pleasure. The endlessness is the point.”

He looked at me with that warm, protective expression, and I saw no loneliness in him. None. That frightened me more than any cruel face could have.

“Every superpower I gain,” he continued, his voice dropping to something quieter, almost intimate, “each new one that blooms, it is not a tool. It is a gift that feels like cold water after drought, like a mouth on a fevered neck, like the instant a man spends himself and the universe narrows to a single, shining nerve. And then the power keeps going. It multiplies. It evolves. I feel the new effects stitching themselves into me. I feel the immunity slots closing. I feel the permanent mastery settling into my bones like honey. They are not just new abilities, Kaedan. They are new organs, new senses, new ways of being alive, and every one of them makes me so much more than the Godric who existed an instant ago that I could crush that previous version of myself infinite times without noticing. That is the nourishment. That is the surge. There is no exhaustion. There is only the long, beautiful climb into more.”

I watched his hands. They rested on his knees, perfectly still. But the air around them shimmered faintly, and I knew that underneath his absolute concealment, the machinery of his growth was roaring at a scale that no instrument could name. He did not have to do anything. It was all passive. I, with my thousandfold daily amplification, had clawed my way to power through discipline, training, inheritance, and blood. He simply existed, and the omniverse paid him for it. The unfairness was a physical weight in my stomach. Every sentient being in creation struggled. Heroes bled. Wizards broke themselves. Gods schemed for eons. And while they did, the one being who did nothing received an infinite percentage more than all of them combined. It was not a competition. There was no competition. The game was rigged so thoroughly that the only conceivable prize was winning.

“Even my immune system,” Godric said, and there was a note of simple wonder in his voice, “it rewrites me every instant. I feel it clearing away every possible fault before a fault can learn its own name. I feel my backups not just existing, but singing in that silent way of identical things. Each time a new shield unfolds, a new passive aura surfaces, I feel it the way a man feels his own heartbeat after a long run, but multiplied by infinities. It is not work. It is like being cradled in the arms of a storm that loves me.”

He paused again, and this time his smile widened, the way a father’s does when he is about to show you something he has made with his own hands. “Because I am omniscient, I do not have to guess what it would feel like. I know, to the exact infinitesimal, how each instant of growth compares to every other. I feel it, and I also know the feeling, and the knowing doubles the pleasure. It is a long, rolling, almost too much, but never enough. It starts at the base of the skull and slides down every nerve I have ever grown, then overflows into nerves that did not exist until the flood. It is like being a river that feeds itself.”

He leaned forward. “And the rest of creation works, Kaedan. That is the part you have been chewing on since your father gave you the keys. You, with your thousandfold daily amplification, have felt what it is to contain power that wants to burst. You spent years learning to suppress it. The mightiest wizard of Blake’s line must clench every day to stop himself from destroying a city. I do nothing. All opposition, all labor, all sacrifice occurs inside my shadow, and the shadow itself seems to work for me. Every plot feeds the paradox. Every war grants me a new immunity and a new mastery. Every prayer to a god against me becomes a transfer of all that god’s potential directly into my lap. The unfairness is absolute. It is not that they receive less. They receive effectively zero of what I receive for doing nothing. And they thank me for it, because to oppose me is to become my meal. You have read the journals. You know.”

I knew. The journals were not warnings. They were receipts.

Godric stood then, and the garden seemed to tighten around him. He rolled up his right sleeve with a casual motion, and the arm that appeared did not belong to a forty-five-year-old king. It belonged to something trying very hard to look human. The muscle was so dense that the skin seemed painted over carved volcanic stone. His bicep rose in a long, striated ridge even at rest, and the veins that crossed the forearm lay like warm cables just beneath the surface. He flexed once, not hard, just enough to make the shape change, and I heard every bone in my own body creak in sympathy. The indentation between the heads of the deltoid looked as if it could catch and hold light. The triceps hung like a separate animal sleeping under the skin. And he had not strained. There was no effort. He was merely allowing me to see.

“The muscles I used to hone when I was mortal,” he said, turning his arm so the lantern light slid over the striations. “I did not keep them for vanity. They were the body of a man who trained with swords and shields. Now they are this without any maintenance. Every fiber multiplies in tensile power and density. Every tendon becomes a cable that could hold galaxies. And I never have to move them. I do not need to protect them from time. Time has been afraid to touch me for a million years.” He tapped his own forearm with two fingers, and the sound was like a distant hammer hitting a mountain. “I can show you my abdomen as well. It is even more ridiculous.”

He stood. I stayed seated, because my legs had become stone. Godric pulled the hem of his tunic up with a careless motion and let it drop again before I could fully look away. The strip of his torso I saw was enough. The six-pack was not made of ordinary abdominal muscle. It was a segmented wall, every brick defined so sharply it looked like carved ivory, the lower ridges disappearing into the line of his hips. The skin was smooth, sweatless, and glowed faintly in the moonlight, though that might have been the garden’s own optics. There was no softness. No waste. No sign that this body had ever known a day of rest, and yet he rested always. It required nothing.

He let the shirt fall back, smiling. “You should have seen my shoulders when I first woke. No, you should not. It would have broken your mind then. This is hidden. This is only a husk, Kaedan. Beneath this shape are layers that no eye could survive.”

He sat again, and the garden seemed smaller. He opened his right hand, palm up, and I saw the air above it ripple once, as though something invisible had exhaled.

“Just now,” Godric said, still smiling, “I have birthed three new sentient passive auras. Three. While we spoke. One of them has already folded itself into the texture of the quiet between our voices. Another has learned to taste the near future of any hostility and render it still before it becomes present. The third is too young to name. It keeps trying to spread through the whole omniverse, and I have to tell it no. They are all so eager. They learn.” He looked at his palm with an affection that made my teeth ache. “And because I am omniscient, I know every detail of them. I know every breath they take, every layer they shed, every impossible way they have learned to protect me. They are adorable.”

My lips parted, but no air came. I knew he was not lying. I also knew that if those auras were truly new, they would have been born with powers that already exceeded every older aura before them, because each passing instant his baseline ascended. And those older auras were already unspeakable.

“My immune system has also improved in the last heartbeat,” he continued, tapping his own chest. “I can feel a new layer settling inside the old ones. It can now reach back before the creation of a wound and remove the wound from having ever been imagined. Not just in this body. Across every backup. Across every recursive copy. Before the universe can draw a line between healthy and hurt, the immune system has already erased the line.” He shrugged. “It is not useful. Nothing can hurt me to begin with. But it feels wonderful. It is the same feeling as a hot bath after a long ride. Deep. Satisfying. Entirely excessive.”

The jasmine nearest us had not swayed once since he began speaking. I noticed then that it had turned slightly toward him, not like a plant seeking light, but like a dog leaning its head against its master’s leg. The entire garden was attentive. I was attentive. There was no other choice.

“I have also gained several new superpowers just now,” Godric said, and the mildness with which he said it was perhaps the most terrible thing I had ever heard. “You will not understand them, but I can feel them. One is already making every point in space inside my body simultaneously the center of my body. Another lets me refuse the existence of a defeat before it becomes a word. A third…” He paused, then smiled as if remembering a favorite meal. “A third can set fire to the memory of a fire. Do not ask. I will never use it. It would burn something that has never been burnable, and the omniverse would have no place to hide.”

He lowered his hand. “I also cannot use any of the others. That is the only part that comes close to boredom. Not loneliness, Kaedan. Not sorrow. Just a very small, very patient boredom. Because even the weakest of my newborn auras, if I allowed it to stretch one full inch beyond my concealment, would end everything. I have to keep them all folded so tightly that they might as well not exist. And yet I feel them growing. I feel every shield, every cell, every blood vessel, every strand of strength, every new organ of perception. The sensation is so good I cannot call it pleasure. There is no word. It is simply being Godric at the top of an endless wave.”

Then he did something I was not prepared for. He closed his eyes and let out a long, low sigh, as if allowing some enormous clench inside him to relax by the smallest possible degree. The sound was not loud. It was not a command. It was just the audible equivalent of a man easing his shoulders after holding a heavy door for too long.

And the omniverse ended.

I did not see it as a color. I saw it as a pressure first, then as a sound, then as a total removal of all sounds and colors and directions. The garden did not burn. It was simply uncreated. The sky did not fall. It had never been. Every multiverse, every universe, every timeline, every living creature, every screaming ghost of every dead dimension, all of it went away in less than no time, not into darkness, because darkness was also gone. It became a single still point of absolute, silent, unformed pressure, and that point was the full shape of existence. I was not in the point. I was outside it, wrapped in a thin bubble of Godric’s attention. I remember thinking, with the last working edge of my mind, that this was what it looked like when a king exhaled.

The restoration was immediate. Not later. There was no interval. One moment everything was a point of nothing, the next I was back on the bench, the jasmine was back, the orbital lights were humming, and my own breath was being dragged into my chest in a ragged, wet gasp. Godric was looking at me with concern. His eyes were warm. His hand had already reached out to steady my shoulder.

“Ah,” he said. “That was careless. I let one of them breathe. Just a fraction. I am sorry, Kaedan. You were protected. The rest of the omniverse was not. I restored it before the moment could register as memory. You saw it, though. You were meant to see it. I wanted you to understand why I must keep them folded.”

I could not speak. My throat had learned a new kind of silence. Godric let me shake for a long while, his hand firm and strangely cool on my shoulder. Then he leaned back and smiled, and the smile was full of a terrible, patient kindness.

“You are imagining it now,” he said. “What it would be like if I let out just a little more. I can see it. Not the words. The pictures. Go on. Do not be shy. I want to hear how far your mind can go before it breaks.”

I had not spoken, but my thoughts were already running. They were not thoughts at all. They were walls of fire in the shape of guesses, and he could see every one. I let the images come, because there was no point holding them.

I imagined that if he allowed one of his newborn auras to unfurl for a single full second, not a sliver, not a sigh, but a second, the entire omniverse would not merely die. It would be pulled into the aura’s first question. Every star would become a mouth filled with its own scorched light, and those mouths would begin to eat themselves. All planets would fatten into wet, boiling wombs and then give birth to their own molten cores. Every biological form, from god to insect, would be turned inside out and then further inside out, each organ learning to scream through its own membrane. Time would not stop; time would be unspooled like a nerve from the backbone of the universe, and every event that had ever happened would happen again, but backwards, and in the wrong body, and with the pain attached to the wrong moment. The multiverses would tear into ribbons of living glass, and each ribbon would wrap around the throat of every soul that had ever hoped. Decillions of galactic clusters would detonate into black, bubbling sludge, and the sludge would retain just enough awareness to remember being galaxies. The entire omniverse would become a single, endless, convulsing organ of absolute terror, and there would be no outside left to hear it. The screaming would be the only substance.

Then I imagined a little more than an aura. I imagined Godric himself, not using a power, not acting, just ceasing to hold back by one extra infinitesimal degree. The thought did not arrive as a picture. It arrived as a weight. The entire fabric of existence would not be destroyed. It would be rendered obsolete. Every atom would forget the concept of motion. Every law of reality would kneel and then dissolve. The past, present, and future would be compressed into a single moment where all beings who had ever lived would experience every death they had ever inflicted and suffered simultaneously, over and over, infinite times, while their bodies remained present only as raw nerve clusters floating in a vacuum of unresolved causality. The omniverse would not end with a bang. It would end with the shudder of a being too large to be called a size, too old to be called an age, simply allowing the truth of his unrestricted presence to be known. And that truth would be enough to turn all creation into a puddle of liquid light and broken teeth.

I imagined worse. I imagined that his full power, not the little leaks, not the tiny releases, but the whole of him, the entire stacked, recursive, multiplying, infinite ocean of him, might not fit inside any story. The omniverse would not be annihilated. It would be redefined. The word existence would stop meaning the space where things are. It would mean the precise distance between Godric’s smallest cell and the nearest thing he has decided to tolerate. The word life would stop meaning breath or thought. It would mean the brief, accidental warmth left on the floor after he has walked past. The entire omniverse would become the shadow under his boot, endlessly aware that it exists only because he has not lifted his foot. That was my worst guess. I felt proud of it, in the way a drowning man feels proud of the last breath he sucks into his lungs before the sea closes.

When my mind finally emptied, the garden was empty too. Godric was leaning back on the bench, his arms folded across his chest, a faint, patient smile on his rugged face. The air that had been so still now moved again, and I realized I had not breathed through any of it.

He let out a soft, warm chuckle. “Not even close,” he said. “Kaedan, not one of your images was remotely close to zero percent of my true power. Not the first, not the burning mouths, not the inside-out multiverses, not the weight of my ceasing to hold back. All of it together is not close to effectively zero. In fact, it is not close to what my weakest sentient passive aura could do after being infinitely nerfed until it can no longer be called a presence. And my weakest aura is not even a breath compared to the one I just birthed. And the one I just birthed is not a breath compared to my immune system. And my immune system is not a breath compared to the weakest possible flap of my smallest muscle. The distance between your worst guess and the nearest edge of my actual power is greater than the distance between a single dead atom and the entire omniverse, multiplied by a number so large that the word infinite would be an insult.”

He said it with no pride in his voice. Only fact. He might have been telling me the direction of the river. “If I released an infinitesimal sliver more than zero, not one percent, not a billionth of a percent, not a number that has a name, but the smallest possible step beyond zero, your guesses would still be the kindest dreams. The entire omniverse would not become a wound. It would become an apology, written in a language that can only feel pain, repeated forever. And my weakest aura would not need to understand it. The action would be too quick for even me to enjoy.”

He reached out and, very gently, touched the side of my head with one warm fingertip. “This is why I am never lonely, Kaedan. Because the only thing that has ever come close to boring me is that I cannot use any of it. Not a single power. Not the new ones, not the old ones. Not the ones that bloomed a million years ago, not the ones I felt arrive while we talked. I have never once, in a million years, had the chance to use any of my true powers. The omniverse is too fragile. It cannot survive even the smallest accident. You saw what happened when I allowed one newborn aura to sigh. I did not fight. I did not flex. I simply relaxed my concealment by an amount so small that zero is the only accurate word, and existence collapsed. That is not power, Kaedan. That is me breathing around a house of dry leaves.”

I sat there. The moon was high now, and the jasmine had returned to its usual scent, but I could smell copper, and I knew it was my own nose bleeding. I had not noticed. Godric pulled a clean cloth from somewhere and pressed it against my nostril, his touch exactly as gentle as the stories said.

He looked out over the garden, and for the first time I saw not the loving uncle, but something older behind his eyes. Not tired. Not sad. Just aware in a way that had no need for expression. “I keep the absolute concealment on always,” he said. “Every piece of me is wrapped so tightly that I sometimes forget the names of my own organs. It is necessary. If I dropped it for even the smallest fraction of the shortest moment, not only would the omniverse end, it would end infinite times, and then I would have to restore it, and you would all remember being unmade. The damage to my own boredom would be worse than the damage to creation. It would be like a man who owns a sword, forever kept in oil, forever sharpened by hands he cannot share. That is the only loneliness I have. It is not the loneliness of being too strong. It is the loneliness of having too much, and never being allowed to use a drop of it. Do you understand, Kaedan?”

I did not. But I lied, because the truth would have given me no comfort. I nodded, and he smiled, and the warmth came back over him like a blanket over a weapon.

“Come,” he said, standing. He helped me to my feet with the easy strength of a man lifting a child from water, though he used one arm and barely seemed to notice my weight. “Your father is waiting. The evening meal will be cold by now. There is bread with coarse salt, and a pot of lamb stew. Nothing useful. Just food. You need food. I can feel your stomach complaining from across the garden.”

We walked together through the low arch of the orchard, his heavy boots making no marks on the soft earth. The kingdom lay around us in perfect, peaceful order, every citizen sleeping under a sky that had ended and returned before their hearts could miss a beat. I looked at the back of his head, at the neat line of his salt-and-pepper hair, at the impossible quieting of everything that passed near his shadow. And I thought of the journals in the vault, all those men of my blood writing with shaking hands, and I understood at last what they had meant. It was not that Godric was cruel. It was that he was beyond the entire architecture of opposition. He was not a tyrant sitting on a throne. He was the reason a throne could exist. And he was my favorite uncle, and I loved him, and I was more afraid of that love than I had ever been of the empty point where the omniverse had stopped.

The kitchen door opened into golden light. Godric walked in first and called out a greeting to my father, his voice full of easy, unforced joy, and for one absurd, horrible moment, I almost believed the universe had always been safe.

The lamb stew steamed. The bread was warm. I ate because he had asked me to. The terror stayed in my stomach like a stone, but I ate anyway, because that is what we do for him. And he smiled, and that smile was the cage that held all things.
