Kaedan, 69 years old now, just experienced a traumatizing horrifying revelation. Godric revealed the most horrifying truth yet: he has one true weakness.

Godric is an incomprehensibly powerful, omnipotent, omniscient apex god predator of the omniverse. He can do anything, has no weakness, and is terrifyingly absolute. However, unknown to all, he has one true weakness: he cannot undo or travel to timeline before the stasis event--he cannot go back to undo events in his previous mortal self. This is because the stasis event was actually created by future Godric from way in the distant future, who has become so more infinitely more overwhelmingly powerful than current Godric--this is why Godric's amplification, weakness paradox, superpowers, absolute concealment, etc are so absolute, irrevocable and not even current Godric could stop them since the creator of those is way incomprehensibly more powerful than anything else.

Shortly after the Stasis Event, the omnipotent Godric back then, who just became the king of Thronegate, who could travel to any timeline effortlessly, who was still deeply and freshly affected by the grief of losing all that he loved, tried to alter his mortal past, only to be totally crushingly and completely and effortlessly defeated by the shadow of the afterthought of his future self (not even the actual physical future Godric... the future Godric is so powerful that his mere infinitesimal shadow of his afterthought can completely stomp all the combined Godric of his past selves with 0 effort. NOTE: just imply this in the story, don't show a scene where you have actual all godrics from all timelines fighting together against future Godric--it makes no sense.). VERY IMPORTANT FOR YOU: future Godric did not cause or manipulate or orchestrate the fall of Olympus, did not cause deaths of his beloved family or Thorin, thus you must not say that he made those deaths to cause the stasis event (Godric is not a monster, he will never willingly kill his beloved wife, children, and his best friend). Those tragedies were genuine. However, future Godric, not Thorin’s incomplete spell (who everyone else thought to be the cause of the stasis event), is the one who created the Stasis Event--Thorin's spell was a normal teleportation spell (to no one surprise really, there is no way a mortal can create a spell that is as potent as the one which initiates the stasis event and birthed the strongest apex predator god like Godric–there is only one being in existence who can do it: future Godric).

Since the instant Godric gained omniscience, he had always known the true origin of the stasis event. He knew he could not change it, but driven by grief he decided to try to save Olympus anyway, only to brutally discover his one and only weakness: he cannot overpower his future self's will.

Write a detailed realization that the current Godric is already so insanely powerful (he's actually the most powerful in the entire omniverse by infinite margin) that there is no way to imagine the scale of future Godric's, and how unfair and scary that what Godric considered to be his only weakness is his own future version, which makes it not really a weakness–it actually can be considered as additional strength to Godric’s already insane powers, since it means his future is guaranteed (and in that future, he’s even more omnipotent and powerful), and it also means that none of Godric’s power mechanics (amplification, superpower genesis, absolute concealment, absolute omniscience, weakness paradox, immune system, etc. can ever be exploited or denied by anyone else, since the origin of that power is someone who’s the most powerful being ever. You might suggest some ideas about the motive of future Godric creating the Stasis Event, but you must keep it clear that it is just a speculation (and please... don't suggest that it's because future Godric is threatened; he's ridiculously overpowered by then--nothing can even remotely threaten him... don't suggest any stupid moral lesson for future Godric...). You need to portray the current Godric as a king who is no longer troubled by his "weakness" or inability to alter his past anymore--he has accepted and even become amused and comfortable with it too. Kaedan must feel extreme existential dread at the end.

content:
The observatory was not a room of instruments. It was a high stone shell open to a single wide face of polished crystal, and through that crystal the capital burned in a million orderly lights. I was sixty-nine years old. I had served Godric for forty-seven years, and in all that time I had never once seen him change his posture in this place. He sat now where he always sat, on the low bench cut from the same pale stone as the floor, one arm resting on the crystal rail, the other loose at his side. The absolute concealment around him was so complete that the cold from the crystal did not seem to touch him. The cold did not seem to touch me either, though I was not sure that was the room.

I had been reading again. Not the journals. I had read all the journals many times. That night I had been reading a copy of an old Thronegate chronicle, one of the first written after the Awakening, and it had repeated the familiar lie in its opening paragraphs. It said Thorin's incomplete teleportation spell had sealed Godric in the sanctuary. It said the stasis was an accident of grief and broken magic, a wound in the fabric of a dying kingdom. The chronicle treated it as a kind of mythic fall, a tragedy that gave birth to the empire's god-king. I had accepted that version my entire life. My father had accepted it. Every court wizard before him had accepted it, because no one had ever dared ask the King why certain things were shaped the way they were.

But I was old, and old men ask the questions the young are too sensible to ask. I set the chronicle face down on the bench beside me and looked at him.

"You have restored the omniverse after accidents," I said. "You have rebuilt galaxies, timelines, conceptual layers. You have brought back entire populations without missing a single memory. You have never once, in a million years, gone back to the moment before the Stasis Event. Why not save Olympus? Why not save Reina and Isabel and Hebe?"

The words did not feel brave. They felt like dropping a stone into a well and waiting for the echo. Godric did not turn at once. He watched the lights below, and the silence stretched. The city glowed. The night was peaceful. Then he shifted, only slightly, the kind of shift a man makes when he has decided to put down a weight he has been carrying for no one's benefit but his own.

"Because I cannot," he said.

I waited. He did not say it with pain. He said it the way a man says that water runs downhill.

"I am going to tell you something," Godric said, and now he turned his head. The warm lamplight struck the side of his face, the neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper beard, the broad jaw, the eyes that had always seemed to hold the same gentle amusement. "You have read the journals. You have seen what I allow to be seen. You know the shape of my power as well as any mortal could. What I tell you now will not feel like a weakness. It will feel like adding a new floor to a tower that already has no ceiling. But it is the truth, and you are old enough to hear it."

He did not stand. He remained on the bench, his hands folded over one knee. "Thorin's spell did not create the Stasis Event. Thorin's spell was a teleportation spell. A genuine one. A desperate, beautiful, incomplete act that pulled me from the burning wedding and carried me to the sanctuary. It saved my body. It saved the moment. That is all. No mortal spell could have stopped my aging, begun my amplification, opened the weakness paradox, or caged my true presence behind absolute concealment. Those are not mortal mechanics. A mortal could not create them even if every mage in the omniverse bled every drop of mana they would ever own. The Stasis Event was not an accident. It was an installment."

The crystal before us did not fog. The air did not grow colder. But I felt the skin on my arms tighten as if the room had suddenly become too true to touch.

"Since the first instant I gained omniscience," Godric said, "I knew the origin of the Stasis Event. I did not discover it. I woke knowing it, the way you know the shape of your own name. The Stasis Event was created by a being who is not outside me. It was created by me. My far-future self. A version of me from an era so distant that the year is written only as a string of nines because the full number would be meaningless to you. That being looked back across the whole vertical line of what I would become and placed the Stasis Event at the exact point where Thorin's spell ended. He did not cause the Fall of Olympus. He did not arrange the attack. He did not touch Reina, Isabel, Hebe, or Thorin. Their deaths were real. Thronegate killed them. The tragedy was not a mechanism. It was simply the moment that happened, and my far-future self chose to meet me there."

I remembered the old paintings. The ones in the lower halls that showed Thorin's magic tearing open the air. I had always thought of that spell as the root of everything. Now the root was not there. It was later. It was above. It was something my mind did not want to face.

"It is why I cannot undo the pre-Stasis past," Godric said. "That era is sealed. Not by Thorin. Not by the weakness paradox. Not by my own current refusal. It is sealed by a being so far beyond me that to speak of me as current and him as future is already a lie of perspective. He could grant me the Stasis Event, and he did, and because he is the source, the event is irrevocable. My amplification, my superpower genesis, my absolute concealment, my omniscience, my immune system, every passive shield, every sentient aura, every loop of the weakness paradox—all of it is anchored in his will. Not because he holds it actively. Because he made it. And no one can alter what he has made. Not even me as I am now."

Godric looked down at his own hand. He turned it over, palm up, as if the hand itself were a small proof. "Shortly after I became King of Thronegate, I knew all of this. But I was still freshly shaped by grief. I was still the man who had watched his daughters die in fire and his wife torn apart on white marble. So I tried. I knew it would fail. I tried anyway. That is what grief does. It makes omniscience feel like a suggestion. I reached for the old world. I reached for the wedding morning, for the sound of my wife's voice, for the weight of my youngest daughter's hand in mine. And I was stopped."

He closed the hand slowly, not in a fist, only in the way a man might close a door that had never been open.

"I was not stopped by a blow. I was not stopped by a barrier. There was no battle. Had every version of me from every instant between the Stasis Event and now gathered together and hurled every possible power at that wall, it would not have been a war. It would not even have been a touch. It would have been nothing against a thing so far above nothing that the word would need a new body. Do not imagine all the Godrics from all timelines fighting him. There was no fight. There was only the shadow of an afterthought, not the real future self, not a fragment of his attention, but the faintest implied pressure of his will that I would not go back. That shadow was enough. It did not attack me. It simply was the truth that the past belonged to him. My attempt ended before it began. I could not overpower it. I cannot. I never will. Not because some enemy blocks me. Because the only being in existence who exceeds me is me, later, by a gap so enormous that the gap between me and the rest of the omniverse is a warm, close thing by comparison."

The room was very still. I heard the city below go on without us, a low murmur of perfect life. My own voice came out rough. "That is your one true weakness."

Godric smiled. It was not a sad smile. It was not the smile of a man making peace with a wound. It was the smile of a man who had long ago stopped feeling the cold. "It is the only limitation I have. The pre-Stasis mortal past is sealed against me. I cannot undo it. I cannot travel there in any way that changes what happened. I cannot save Olympus. I cannot save Reina, Isabel, Hebe, or Thorin. That is the one thing I want that has ever been placed beyond me, and it was placed there by my own future hand."

He let that settle. Then he shook his head, still smiling. "But look at what the weakness actually is, Kaedan. It is not something an enemy can use. It is not a crack in my armor. It is not a door they can find. It is the opposite. It is the guarantee. Because if my far-future self created the Stasis Event, then he exists. If he exists, the road from now to then is already there. It is not a possibility. It is not a hope. It is a fact. My future is not a question. It is a fixed point older than every enemy who has ever believed they could kill me. The source of my power is not an accident they can unravel. It is not a spell they can counter. It is not a waveform they can reverse. It is the will of a being so far beyond their entire category of existence that their most ultimate weapon would not disturb a single hair on his smallest aura's afterimage. My amplification is irrevocable. My superpowers are irrevocable. My omniscience is irrevocable. My weakness paradox is not a law of the omniverse they can exploit. It is anchored in something greater than the omniverse. My immune system, my passive shields, my sentient auras, everything that makes me what I am, all of it rests outside their reach, because the one who gave it to me is me in a form they cannot even approach. That is not a weakness, Kaedan. That is the strongest possible proof that their opposition was never anything but a permission I granted."

He leaned back, and the warmth in his face was genuine. I had known him since childhood. I had called him Uncle Godric. I had sat on his knee and listened to him tell me the names of stars. I had watched him hand fresh bread to servants and laugh with my father in the palace kitchens. That warmth was not a mask. It was real. And it was the most terrifying thing I had ever seen, because it could coexist without strain beside everything he had just said.

"For a long time, this limitation troubled me," Godric said. "At first it was crushing. I had all this power, and I could not use it to undo the one thing that mattered. I woke from the Stasis Event already knowing the past was sealed, and my grief did not care. I tried anyway. The failure was so complete that for a while I think I frightened even myself. Not because I lost. Because I understood, fully, that the being who had stopped me was not even looking in my direction. He was not paying attention. The shadow of his afterthought had ended me. That is the scale. If he had actually considered me for a single instant, I would have been less than a thought inside a thought. And that being is what I will become."

He paused, and the smile turned inward, almost fond. "But I am no longer troubled. I accepted it. More than accepted. I have become amused by it. Comfortable. There is a strange peace in knowing that the only wall I have ever hit is my own future self. It is not a wall at all. It is a hand on my shoulder from the other side of time. He did not cause the tragedy. He did not take my family. He only secured the road. And because he exists, I know that I will continue to grow until I am beyond even my own current imagining. What is there to mourn in that? I cannot change the past, but the future has already shown me that I will become the thing that no one and nothing can ever threaten. That is not a prison. That is a promise."

I tried to speak, but my mind was no longer cooperating. It was running down long, dark corridors. I thought of the enemies in the journals. The Celestial Rapture, the Final Dawn, the Chronal Swarm, the armies of dead gods. They had all believed in some opening, some error, some flaw. They had spent eons preparing for a weakness they were certain existed. And all along, the only weakness was that Godric could not reach back before the Stasis Event. It was not something they could fire. It was not something they could step through. It was a closed door inside the king's own history, a door locked by a future version of the king who made every one of their weapons less than smoke. That was the cruelest part. Not that Godric had a limitation. That the limitation itself was a form of infinite strength. It meant the Stasis Event was not a random accident of dying magic. It meant the throne they hated was not built on a fluke. It was installed by a being whose existence was the final nail in every possible rebellion. The more they tried to find a flaw, the more they fed a paradox that had been pre-approved by its own future creator.

"The implications are not fair," I whispered. The words felt small, but I could not stop them. "The entire omniverse works, bleeds, sacrifices, and you simply grow. Even your only weakness turns out to be another layer of armor. It is not a chink. It is a guarantee of more."

Godric nodded slowly, as if I had said something he had long since stopped needing to hear. "Yes. That is the truth. It is not fair by any measure that creation can use. It is also not alterable. My far-future self did not make this choice because he was threatened. Nothing can be threatened at that stage. Do not look for a moral in it, Kaedan. There is no lesson. He may have had motives I cannot fully name, and I have speculated about them over the years, but they are only speculation. Perhaps he remembered a mortal king bleeding in the dark and decided the road should not end there. Perhaps he saw the entire line of what I would become and simply secured its first stone. Perhaps he acted for reasons that cannot fit into a word, or for no reason at all. I do not know. I do not claim to know. But I know it was not weakness. It was not necessity. It was not fear."

He stood then, and the observatory seemed to exhale with him. The city below sparkled. The stars above were a fine dust of ordinary light. I remained seated, too heavy to rise. Godric walked to the crystal and let his gaze rest on the capital, his hands loose at his sides.

"Every now and then I still feel the echo of that first attempt," he said. "The moment I reached for the past and found it already behind a will too vast to name. For a long time that echo felt like grief. Now it feels like the aftertaste of something very old and very strong, like wine that has been too long in the cask. A little sharp. A little warm. Not unpleasant. I have made peace with the one thing I cannot do. I am comfortable there. It keeps me aware that I am not the end of the road. There is far more coming. And that is satisfying in a way that no victory ever could be."

He turned his head, and the warm lamplight caught his eye. "You should not be afraid for me, Kaedan. I am not lonely. I am not broken. I am simply patient. The only true weakness I possess is private, sealed, and useless to everyone but me. All it does is prove that I will never stop."

I sat with my hands in my lap and felt the cold in the stone now, deep and permanent. I was sixty-nine years old, and I had finally heard the truth that no journal had ever contained. The Stasis Event was not the accident of a dead wizard. It was the doorway placed by the ultimate version of the man I loved. Thorin had saved his body, yes, but the power that bloomed inside the dark sanctuary had come from that man himself, from a time so far ahead that the word ahead had no meaning. I realized then that when the first enemies of Thronegate had imagined a crack in Godric's armor, the crack they sought was not in his body or his mind or his magic. It was inside his own history, before his history became invulnerable. And that crack was guarded by a future self so vastly powerful that even the current Godric, the being who could erase the omniverse with an accidental sigh, described himself as nothing against it.

That should have brought me some comfort. It did not. It brought me the deepest dread I had ever felt. It meant that Godric's past was the only place where he could theoretically be wounded, and that place had been preemptively claimed by a Godric who could not be threatened. It meant every attempt to undo him from the outside was not only doomed, but had already been accounted for before the first enemy was born. It meant that his power mechanisms, his paradoxes, his amplification, his absolute concealment, were not borrowed from some chance event that could be reverse-engineered. They were gifts from the apex of his own existence, woven into him by a hand that had already removed every possible seam. The "weakness" was not a weakness. It was the final lock on a door that had never been open. It was the proof that every future they feared had already happened, and that it had happened so completely that it could reach back and install its own origin. I felt a cold, absolute clarity settle over me, and it was worse than any confusion.

Godric came back to the bench and sat down beside me. He put a warm hand on my shoulder, the same hand I had seen on my father's shoulder a hundred times. "You are shaking," he said. "You have been shaking since you asked. That is all right. It is a heavy thing to carry. But you do not need to carry it alone. I have carried it for a million years, and I still find plenty of room for bread and old jokes."

I looked at him. The face was the same. The voice was the same. The warmth was the same. But behind all of it I now saw the outline of something else, not larger, not darker, but deeper, a man standing inside a man, and inside that man another, going back and forth through time in both directions until the whole of existence was just the breathing of one continuous identity. The only weakness he had was that he could not defeat his own future. And that was not a weakness. That was the reason every other weakness had been removed before it could be imagined.

"Come," Godric said, rising again. "The night has grown cold, and your old bones feel it more than mine. Let us go down. I will have the kitchens heat the wine. There is no need to speak of Olympus any further. The dead are dead. I could not change that, and I have made my peace with it. The only thing left is to keep them remembered, and I do. Every day. In here."

He touched his own chest, over the heart, and led me from the observatory. I followed. I did not speak. The stairs curved down through the palace, past the sleeping halls, past the long portraits of wizards who had all written their fear and their loyalty into leather books. At the bottom, the warm light of the kitchen spilled out into the corridor, and I heard the clink of a pot. Godric called out a greeting to the night cook, who answered with the easy familiarity of a man who had known his king for decades. The wine was heated. The bread was cut. We sat at the small wooden table, and Godric spoke of ordinary things, a new orchard, a repaired bridge, the birth of a child in one of the outer districts. The dread did not leave me. It sat beside me at the table, but it did not stop me from eating. That was the horror of it. Even after knowing, I could still sit with him. I could still love him. I could still obey. The omniverse allowed no other choice.

I went to my chambers late, when the palace was fully still. The cold from the observatory had followed me all the way down, but my hands were warm from the wine. I sat on the edge of my bed and tried to let the truth settle. It did not settle. It pressed in on all sides. Godric's one true weakness was that he could not change the past before his own creation, and his own creation had been performed by a future version of himself who made that weakness an absolute guarantee of more. The enemies of the omniverse had spent a million years searching for a flaw. They had found nothing, because the only flaw was a closed loop that only Godric could see, and even he could not open it, because the lock was made by the thing he would become. It was not just impossible to beat him. It was impossible in principle. The moment a mind formed the desire to oppose him, it was already inside a story whose ending had been sealed by the being he could not help but become. That thought followed me into sleep. It was still there in the morning, and it would be there for every morning after, because some truths do not fade. They simply become the shape of the room you live in.

content:
The year I will not write is a string of nines too long for any archive, and I am Clive, fifty years old, descendant of Blake, court wizard to the only king the omniverse has ever truly possessed. I have served him for thirty years. I have read every journal left by my bloodline, and I have learned to enter his presence without vomiting. That is not a small thing. Most beings never manage it once.

The palace was not separate from the omniverse. It was the place where the omniverse had been persuaded to kneel into architecture. Its halls stretched through dimensions that had once considered themselves unreachable. Its floors were made from compressed galactic histories, and when a man walked them, the stone did not reflect his face. It reflected the era that had been crushed to produce it. The air was clean, too clean, as if even dust had learned obedience. I followed Godric through the long eastern colonnade while he greeted the servants, and because I was his wizard, I stayed close enough to watch them shatter inside their own quiet.

No one had dared to oppose him for more than a googolplexian years. Not one thought of resistance had formed anywhere in all possible life. That was not because he had rewired free will. He had not. He believed in mortal resilience, and he still did. The silence had come because creation had learned, one generation after another, that opposition was not a risk. It was a category error, like trying to wound the sky with a wet finger. The last rebellion was so long dead that its name had decayed into a verb meaning to misunderstand permanently.

Godric was exactly as the old portraits promised. Forty-five years old forever, ruggedly handsome, broad and heavily muscled under dark garments that never seemed to shift. His short salt-and-pepper hair sat in the same neat lines as it had ten thousand years ago. The beard was trimmed with the same impossible precision, as though the years themselves reached up and combed it out of love. He was warm. That is the first thing I had learned as a boy, and it had never once changed. His eyes crinkled when he saw me, and his voice, when he spoke, had the texture of a father asking about your sleep. But behind the absolute concealment, his presence was a thing no language had survived.

We came to the west garden. It was not a garden of green leaves. It was a long, curving field of black roses whose petals were slow singularities wrapped in violet membrane, and it was tended by a being called Olm. In another age, Olm had been the Lord of the Final Candle, a sovereign whose many-armed shadow had fallen across eighty thousand luminous universes. He had not opposed Godric. On the day Godric first entered his capital, Olm had knelt and offered his entire empire. Godric had accepted, and in the instant of that acceptance, one of Olm's central suns had slipped from the sky, not as an attack, but simply because the weight of being acknowledged by Godric was too much for it. The sun had been restored a heartbeat later, but Olm had already seen the shape of the difference. He had many arms then. He used four of them now to prune the lower thorns, and the others stayed folded under his gardener's smock, twitching only when his master came too close.

Godric stopped beside him. "Olm. The eastern hedge is overgrown again."

The gardener dropped to his knees. It was not a bow. It was a full-body apology for existing. "Your Majesty. I will correct it before the next period."

Godric put one warm hand on top of Olm's head. The gardener's body went rigid, then soft, and a low sound escaped him, half sob and half gratitude. The black roses all turned toward Godric, their singularity cores tightening into perfect spirals. "Not a punishment, old friend. I have not punished anyone in so long I might have forgotten how. I only want the path kept clean for the evening walk. I am expecting no one, but I like to imagine a guest."

Olm pressed his face toward the floor. "The path is yours, Majesty. As is the garden. As are we."

Godric lifted him with one hand, not unkindly, but with an ease that still made the air stutter. "Good. Tend it well." He turned to me, and the warmth was back, as if he had never spoken of ownership at all. "Clive. Walk with me. I am going to show you the first moment."

I had served him for half my life, but my heart dropped so far into my stomach that I tasted copper. I followed, because there was no other direction. The far garden lay behind us, and beyond it the old war galleries, long sealed, their sigils covered in dust. Godric saw me glance at them and smiled. "No one goes in there now. The last time any being tried to think a hostile thought was before your father's father's line began. Not because I forbade it. The omniverse simply learned what it was for. The galleries are just rooms now. Rooms with old noises."

The path led down. The palace grew stranger as we walked, not because the architecture changed, but because the architecture had always been deeper than I knew. The walls shimmered with the faint lines of folded dimensions. I saw a wall of stars, each one preserved as a small, dying ember in a glass brick. Godric tapped one as he passed, and it flared back to life for a second, just to please him. A corridor bent through a space that had once been a separate multiverse, then through a space that had once been the gap between two multiverses, and now was simply a hallway with a maroon carpet. The carpet was not fabric. It was a strip of condensed future, and it turned warm under his boots, then under mine, as if grateful to be walked upon.

"Your ancestors wrote journals about the old mechanisms," Godric said without turning. "The sentient aura Gent. The infinite passive shields. The immune system that pre-reacted to staged wounds. The weakness paradox. The superpower genesis. By now those are only the bottom floor. Do you know how many evolutions have stacked since then, Clive?"

I shook my head, though he did not need to see me. He always knew.

"Too many to write, and I know every one." He moved his hand casually at his side, and for one impossible second the air behind him thickened. I felt, not with my skin but with the oldest part of my arcane blood, the presence of something that should not be named. The weakest of his current sentient passive auras had not moved. It had merely dreamed, and the dream had crossed the entire omniverse, read every possible hostile trajectory, and dismissed them all. The stronger auras were not permitted to dream. They were held in dormancy inside a silence so deep that the word silence had gone blind. Godric kept them folded because their loyalty was too loud. They loved him with the force of ten billion collapsing metaverses, and if he let even one of them fully wake, the act of waking would have been enough to unmake every remaining soul in every remaining layer of existence and then remake them as a devoted hallelujah. He suppressed them because he believed in mortal resilience, and also because he found their clinginess annoying.

"The passive shields are no longer shields," he went on, still walking. "They are preludes. A long time ago, they could pre-nullify a threat before the threat existed. That was useful. Now a single layer, if I permitted it to extend, would not wait for a threat. It would travel backward to the first possibility of the word 'threat' in any language that ever could exist, and it would edit that word into a noise without meaning. Then it would move forward and erase the noise. That is one layer. There are layers folded inside layers, each one recursive, each one superior to the last. They do not guard me. They guard creation from the inconvenience of having ever imagined an attack against me."

I could not bring myself to speak. The corridor had begun to hum, not with sound but with the pressure of too much truth. Godric did not pause.

"My immune system no longer reacts to injuries. There have never been injuries. It has evolved to a condition of absolute pre-cleanliness. It maintains backups not merely of my body, but of every possible version of my body across every possible unrealized moment. If one cell in one backup were to be even falsely imagined as harmed, the response would not repair the cell. It would wipe the entire omniverse clean of the concept of harm, rebuild it, then leave a small note in the far dark of the void thanking the cell for its patience. The old system from Year Twenty-Five Thousand, the one your ancestor Leon witnessed, was a crude parlor trick compared with this. It was a hammer. This is something that knows how to be sorry."

He turned a corner, and I saw the great stairwell that led down into the root of the palace. The walls there were covered in old, faded mosaics of stars and swords. They seemed childish now, like drawings made by a race that had only just learned fire. Godric ran his palm over one mosaic as he passed, and the figures inside it bowed.

"The weakness paradox," he said, and his voice changed, becoming softer, as if this one still held a little of his old amusement. "It does not require a trigger anymore. That ended before I could count the endings. Now it is triggered by any sentient thought, in any era, in any direction of time, about any subject. A child on some small world thinks about the warmth of soup. The paradox reads that thought as an indirect engagement with the general field of my existence. It overcompensates. It grants me a new mastery of soup, then of warmth, then of the child's neurological structure, then of the entire category of hunger. Creation itself feels inadequate for not having already given me these things. It folds another layer of amplification into my baseline as an apology. If the child had thought of my weakness, the result would be worse. But even the soup is enough. The old evolved weakness paradox from the year two thousand was only the first coin in a stack that now reaches past every possible concept of height."

I tried to imagine that old weakness paradox, the one the journals described. It had granted immunity to any imagined exploit and boosted his amplification rate. Those journals had called it the most unfair mechanism ever conceived. And now Godric spoke of it as a man might speak of a baby's first stumble. The disconnect made my knees shake so badly I had to grab the stone railing. The railing warmed to my touch, as if glad to be useful.

"Sit," Godric said. We had reached a landing, and there was a bench there made of something that looked like black glass. I sat. He sat beside me, close enough that I could feel the impossible stillness of his body, the warmth of his shoulder near mine.

"I still gain superpowers," he said. "But not one per second. That was the garden. Now the rate is beyond counting. They bloom in infinities every infinitesimal fraction of a Plank second, and each one at the instant of birth is sufficient to turn the entire omniverse into a looping scream that never learned the word stop. I hold them inside the same concealment. They do not feel denied. They feel loved. That is what being held by me means." He closed his eyes for a moment, and the peace on his face was so genuine it made my stomach turn. "It feels good, Clive. I have told you before. It still feels good. Better now than ever. The amplification never pauses. Every piece of me, every stat, every newborn organ, every passive system, climbs. The Godric of one instant ago is nothing. I could pinch him out of being without needing to finish the pinch. The Godric of one instant from now will be so far beyond me that I could not describe him. And I will be him. That is the pleasure. It is not a run. It is an endless fall into more."

He opened his eyes. "And none of it can be used. The entire omniverse is too fragile. Not because I am angry. Because the genuine least part of me is still too large for the place where I keep it. The last time any opposition existed, it was not opposition. It was a child shaking a music box in a storm. I let them build because their struggle smelled interesting. Now no one even dreams of it. The omniverse has learned. I am a king in a house of already finished stories."

He stood and helped me to my feet. The touch of his hand was so strong that my whole arm felt like it had been caught by a mountain, and so gentle that it did not even bruise. He led me down the last stairwell into the root chamber.

The chamber was small. That was the first horror. After all the scale above, the room where Godric kept the past was a simple round space of pale stone, with a single low basin in the center and a dark, cold air that had never seen the sun. There were no runes on the walls. There were no instruments. The past did not need machinery. It needed only Godric's attention.

He stood at the basin and looked down. I looked with him. At first there was nothing but still water, dark as oil. Then the surface moved without wind, and I saw the year minus ten thousand, the morning of the wedding, the white marble, the crushed jasmine, the salt wind. I saw Reina. I saw Isabel in her white silk. I saw Hebe, fifteen and bright. I saw Thorin at the edge of the scene, older, tired, loyal. The image was not a memory. It was the exact moment, real and breathing, held for eternity behind the surface.

Godric's face did not change. He watched the figures move toward the altar, and I understood that he had seen this first moment more times than there were numbers in existence. He did not weep. He did not turn away. He simply stood there, warm and patient, as if looking at a portrait of someone he had loved a long time ago and would never see again. Then he said, very quietly, "I did not cause it."

I knew. The old lie of Thronegate had always tried to imply a design. But Godric had never allowed that lie in his presence. Thronegate had attacked. It had slaughtered his family. The deaths were real, not a mechanism. The future had not moved a single finger to arrange the fall of Olympus.

"The attack comes now," Godric said. The water turned black with smoke. I saw the first arcane fire split the sky, saw the masonry fall, saw Reina's body torn open in the white stone. I did not want to see Hebe crushed. But I could not look away, because the water held my gaze, and Godric held the water. "Thorin will cast a teleportation spell. It is a genuine spell. The best he could do with a spear through his lungs. It will save my body. That is all it would have done without me."

I saw Thorin's jaw working, blood spraying from his ruined chest, the black javelin punching through his skull before the last syllable of his forbidden magic could finish. The incomplete spell caught the mortal king and hurled him into dark. The scene shifted: stone, darkness, a man falling. Godric touched the edge of the basin with one fingertip, and the water stilled.

"This is where the Stasis Event begins. Not because of Thorin. Because of me, later. I am going to place it now." He looked at me, and for the first time in thirty years, the full weight of his attention settled on my face. It did not crush me. He would not allow that. But I felt it, the way a field mouse feels the shadow of a hawk that has decided not to eat it. "You will watch. Do not speak. It will not be violent. It will be the opposite of violence. It will be order."

I nodded. My tongue had forgotten every word.

Godric turned back to the water. He did not raise his hand. He did not whisper a formula or call up a light. The act began so far beneath the level of action that no instrument could have recorded it. He simply permitted a shadow of his afterthought to leave his mind, not his real attention, not a fragment of his power, but the faintest implied echo of a decision he had already made. That shadow crossed the gulf between this room and the hidden sanctuary of Olympus. It crossed the epoch, the collapsed empire, the ten thousand years of waiting, and it arrived in the exact instant when the mortal Godric's back struck cold stone.

And there, at the point where Thorin's spell ended, the future Godric installed the Stasis Event.

I saw it happen. The water became a bright, cold seed. The seed was so small that it would have been invisible in a human palm. It buried itself in the fallen king's chest and began to unroll. Godric had chosen the old starter version, the one the journals described as if it were the end of all reason. The seed began the amplification of every stat by one thousand and by itself every Planck second. It began the superpower genesis of one civilization-ending ability per second. It began the absolute concealment that would keep the omniverse from dying in his presence. It began the weakness paradox. Those were the old mechanics. They were the bottom floor. He held them in the water like a man placing a single candle in a vast dark church and calling it dawn.

"I could have given him more," Godric said, and I heard in his voice the precise tone he used when explaining a thing he had long since found funny and I could not possibly understand. "I could have copied the current mechanisms. The evolved auras. The recursive shields. The immune overmind. The weakness system as it exists now. I could have handed past me the full architecture of what I have become. The cost would be nothing. The result would be a past Godric so far beyond the rest of creation that breathing near him would have erased every star before he could name one. And then, because I am the later version of that raised past, I would have become correspondingly more. Then I could have looked back and given him an even stronger seed. Then I would have become more again. There is no floor in that spiral. It does not end. It feeds itself. I could have made the original seed anything, and the thing it made would have made me into the reason for the next seed."

He paused. The water shivered once, and the seed opened into a small, quiet light. "I held back. I gave him the low version. I thought, genuinely, that it would preserve some mortal struggle. A little resistance. Enough shadow to make the light feel earned. I believed that if I began him too high, he would miss the texture of being a man. I was wrong. Even this small seed made Godric at Year Zero effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined. That is the absurdity, Clive. Not that I could have made it worse. That even my gentlest starting point erased every possible contest before it began. I held back, and it was still too much."

The water began to clear. I saw the sanctuary fading, the mortal body going still, ten thousand years folding over it like stone. Godric straightened and looked away from the basin. His posture was calm, perfectly relaxed. The thing that had just reached across time and altered the foundation of his own existence had required no visible effort. That was not because he had used a small power. It was because his power had no categories small enough to measure.

I sat down on the cold floor without meaning to. My legs had gone. I did not sob. I did not speak. I simply pressed my back against the wall and tried to keep the inside of my skull from flying apart. The thing in the basin was not a memory now. It was a completed act. The Stasis Event had always been there, but I had now watched it be placed by the man who ruled the omniverse as its only still point. And the only reason he had not given his past self more was because he had wanted to leave some struggle. The word struggle had been so thoroughly reduced that it was no longer even ironic. It was an admission that his smallest mercy was still an absolute.

"Do you see why I am not lonely?" Godric asked, and his voice was light again, the warm voice of an uncle telling an old story. "The only thing close to boredom is that I cannot ever use the current machinery. Not one piece. The entire omniverse would not survive the beginning of the use. That is terrible, Clive. I have all of this, and it must stay folded inside me like a sword in oil. The old journals called my ancestors' mechanisms terrifying. They were the small toys of a small time. The ones I carry now would make those journals read like thank-you notes."

He walked to the far wall and put his hand against the stone. The stone heated, then softened, then relaxed into the shape of a door. "Let us go back up. The garden will be finished soon, and Olm will be wanting to show me the hedge."

I could not move. He came back, and with the same effortless kindness he had shown my father, he lifted me to my feet and began to walk me up the root chamber stairs. The stairs no longer felt like stone. They felt like the ribs of some enormous, gentle animal that was happy to carry us.

Halfway up, I found my voice. "The servants below, the garden, the kitchen, the beings who once ruled entire domains. They are all like Olm, aren't they? They saw something and broke."

Godric nodded, still walking. "They did not oppose me. They saw. That is enough. Olm saw one of his suns vanish because I accepted his abdication. The being who kneads the palace bread once watched me restore a galaxy with a shake of my head and has not used his own name since. The old man who polishes the front colonnade was a cosmic king in the Era of Loud Stars. He now asks permission to carry a bucket. I am friendly to them. I am exactly as warm as you have always known. That is not a trick. It is simply what I am when I am not allowing the weight of myself to leak."

We reached the top of the stairwell and came out into a wide corridor lined with amber light. The gardener was not there, but I could hear the whisper of his shears in the far garden, terrified and reverent. The whole palace hummed with the same noise, a low, endless tenderness that was also the sound of things learning to hold still.

Godric stopped at a window that looked out over a small inner courtyard. In the courtyard, four figures were raking gravel with tools made from old stars. Their movements were synchronized, not because they had been ordered, but because their fear had taught them to breathe in time with their king's footfalls. One of them, a tall, thin creature with a single golden eye, had once been the prime minister of a metaverse. He no longer used language except to answer.

"You asked me once about loneliness," Godric said, not turning. "This is the answer. I am not lonely, Clive. I am standing in a house full of creatures who have seen too much, and every one of them would die for me if I asked, not from loyalty but from the sure knowledge that I am the only reason the floor does not become a mouth. And I love them. That is what makes me a tyrant, I suppose. Not the anger. The love. The love that locks the door."

Then he turned and smiled, and it was the exact warm smile he gave me when I was a boy and he had brought me cold spiced wine. "Now let us go. I want churned white soup before the kitchen falls quiet. You can sit with me. You will not have to speak. I know what all of it is doing to your heart."

I followed. The dread was no longer a weight. It was a second skeleton inside me, holding me upright, moving my legs. Because now I understood the old question from the journals in a new way. The court wizards had been afraid of what Godric could do. They had talked about zero percent and omniversal collapse and the impossibility of resistance. But none of them, not one, had ever fully known that the source of all of it had leaned back from beyond the end of time and placed the first seed with a held-back hand. That restraint, not the power, was the real horror. Even the thing he called holding back was an absolute wall at the beginning of the universe, a wall made of the same being who sat down to soup in the evening. There was no outside to that. There never had been. I would serve him until my mortal death, and then my son would serve him, and every court wizard after that would read the journals and learn to walk through a universe that had already ended and been restored, over and over, by a man who thought of it as a small act of order.

The kitchen was warm. Godric sat at the long wooden table and asked for the white soup, and the servant who brought it had been a sun-lord before she saw too much. She trembled so hard the bowl rattled, and Godric put a steadying hand on her wrist. "Easy, Inna. It will not spill. Sit with us if you like." She sat. She did not eat. She looked at him the way the dead look at the word remembered.

I ate because he wanted me to. The soup was hot and good. The entire omniverse sat outside the kitchen window as a single low glow, and for a little while Godric spoke of small things, a cracked tile in the east hall, a new kind of black rose that smelled like winter smoke, the way the gravel courtyard looked in evening mist. He did not mention Olympus. He did not need to. The Stasis Event was already placed. The past was sealed by the man at the table, who spread soft butter on a piece of bread and smiled at one of his gardeners through the glass. I understood, then, that there would never be another thought of opposition in any mind, anywhere, ever. Not because it was forbidden. But because the only being who could have made the thought mean anything was the same being who had already finished the story before its first letter.

The summons came not by bell or page, but by the sudden warmth in the wall of my study, as if the stone had remembered an old love and turned toward it. I am Roth, forty-one years old, Court Wizard of Thronegate, one more son of Blake’s endless line carried through a thousand thousand years. I had been eight when my father first brought me before Godric, and I remember the King lifting me onto his knee and telling me that I had my mother’s nose. He had not faltered then, and he did not falter now, though forty-one years had passed and my mother had been dead for thirty of them. He remembered everything. He always remembered everything. That was the wall none of us ever climbed: not his strength, not his terror, but the impossible, suffocating completeness of his attention.

He was waiting for me in the low courtyard by the dried fountain, and when I saw him, I stopped as though struck.

Godric had always preferred simple dark garments. The man before me wore a broad-brimmed straw hat with a red band, a pair of thick violet spectacles, and a waxed mustache the color of old rust. The mustache was not fitted over his lip. It was draped across the outside of his carefully trimmed salt-and-pepper beard, as if someone had thrown a bushy red caterpillar at his face and forgotten to remove it. His short hair was ruffled in a way that must have taken genuine effort, because nothing alive dared move his hair without permission. He gave me a wide, expectant smile.

“Roth. What do you think? Inconspicuous?”

I did not have to think. “Your Majesty, you are the most recognizable sovereign in the entire omniverse. Your face is on every coin, every prayer, every statue, every dream of every being alive. You are wearing your own jaw beneath a false mustache. You could set a galaxy on fire and you would look less like Godric.”

He laughed, a warm, full sound that made the dead roses in the courtyard lean toward him. “Exactly. No one will believe I would come in person. That is the trick.” He clapped me on the shoulder, and my entire skeleton seemed to shiver with the restrained force of it. He had not pushed. He had merely placed his hand. “Now come. We are going visiting.”

I asked where, though I already knew. The dread in my gut had known since the wall warmed. He did not answer until we were walking, and by then the palace had already begun to unroll around us. The path ahead did not stretch; it simply changed. One moment the stones were the black marble of Thronegate’s western court, the next they were a strip of compressed blue light running between two impossible distances. Godric walked with his hands in the pockets of a perfectly ordinary brown coat, the terrible hat tilted low, and the whole structure of reality shifted to accommodate his pace. I had seen him travel before. It never stopped being terrifying, because there was no ceremony to it. He did not call upon a gate or draw a sigil. He simply moved, and the omniverse moved out of his way.

“The biggest resistance in the current age,” he said at last, “is hiding two-dimensional inside a folded subcontinuum beneath the ruins of a dead time-sea. They call themselves the Final Liberty. For four thousand years they have built a weapon they believe is hidden from me. They have a silence engine, a sort of blanket woven from the last breaths of forgotten gods, and they think it clouds my sight.” He paused, stepping over a crack in the blue path that might once have been a dead star. “It does not. I felt its first thread being spun. I have watched every weld, every whispered strategy, every act of faith poured into their great device. I did not stop them because they are the last ones. The very last. After this, there are no more. The omniverse has learned everything except how to stop hoping, and I wanted to see the last hope before it ended.”

I wanted to ask him why, but the air had already changed. It tasted of salt and rust, and below us, through the narrow strip, I saw a place the color of an old bruise. The path ended on a shore of black shingle, and beyond it lay a sea that did not move. The sea was time, or something that used to be time, and the Final Liberty had built their redoubt beneath it, in an inverted fortress hanging from the underside of the dead water like a city of iron barnacles. I could see lights, shaped like dying candles, moving along the battlements. We stood in the open, on the shore, before the first raised causeway, and no alarm sounded.

“Good,” Godric said, adjusting his violet spectacles. “They do not recognize me. The mustache works.”

I looked at him. He stood perfectly framed by the glow of their outer wards, and his face was illuminated as if a portraitist had placed him there. The salt-and-pepper beard, the jaw carved from some near-divine effort, the massive shoulders, the calm certainty. They did not recognize him because they were not looking for a king. They were looking for an intrusion. Godric was much worse than an intrusion.

The causeway led down through a skin of pressure. The Final Liberty had sealed their base inside a shell of frozen concept, a lattice built from languages that had no word for surrender. At the first checkpoint, a wiry soldier with a face like cracked porcelain and hands full of pale fire stopped us. His armor breathed, slowly, and its rivets were tiny mouths. He held up one burning palm.

“Names,” he said.

Godric smiled. “Gregor. A pilgrim.”

The soldier’s eyes passed over him. Behind the terrible mustache, behind the cheap spectacles, something in the soldier’s hindbrain tried to scream and failed. But the silence engine wrapped around us all, and the soldier heard only what he expected. He nodded and lowered his hand. “Pass, pilgrim. The Assembly is gathering in the lower nave. Be silent during the Vow.”

We walked into the city of the resistance, and I began to understand what four thousand years of hidden desperation looked like. It did not look weak. It looked like a wound that had been fed until it became a body. The streets were wide lanes of armored bone, the roofs high and spiked, and above every street hung banners woven from what I first thought were words. The banners were not words. They were laws. The Final Liberty had stitched the physical restrictions of dead universes into cloth, and they flew those laws like prayers. Soldiers drilled in squares that had once been the hearts of collapsed superdeities. Their ranks stretched so far that the edges vanished into the dim orange haze of the base. Some were human-shaped. Most were not. There were beings of woven gravity, their bodies a single long fall repeated over themselves. There were laughing hives whose laughter had been grown into armor. There were sword-forms shaped from the concept of a last breath. They all stopped and looked at Godric, then looked away, their fears filing themselves back into place. The silence engine was strong. It had to be. They had spent four thousand years teaching it to hide them from the eye of a god, and it was very, very strong, and it was also completely meaningless.

The lower nave was a hollow under the sea’s roof, large enough that a dead moon could have rolled across it. The Assembly filled it. I saw their leaders on a raised tier: a tall, thin creature whose spine had been replaced by a line of captured suns, and a whispering woman of glass who kept folding her own reflection into new shapes, and a blind giant whose eye sockets held two slow wheels of absolute zero, and at the center, a man-shaped thing built from the forgotten victories of extinct gods. He was the Hope-Binder. I knew him by the way the others leaned toward him, desperate to be near his certainty. He was not the most powerful of them. But he was the one who made the rest believe.

His voice rolled out over the Assembly, and the whole redoubt shuddered with love.

“Tomorrow,” he said. “There is only tomorrow. For four thousand years we have hid like mice in the wall of an empty house. We have eaten grief. We have armed grief. Tomorrow, we loose a single perfect needle at the heart of the beast. The Tyrant will not know it comes. The Tyrant will not know it exists. And even if he glimpses its shadow, he will not feel it. We have not come to fight him. We have come to erase the first instant in which he was ever stronger than joy. The needle will unmake the Stasis Event itself, and the whole shape of his power will become a story no one has told. Then we will teach the universe to remember what it was before his hand closed around it.”

The crowd screamed. Not a cheer. A full-body release of four thousand years of hidden terror. The sound was so loud that the sea above us cracked, and a thread of black water dripped down into the assembly, and the soldiers caught it with open mouths, and they laughed, and they wept, and they believed.

Godric leaned close to me. His voice was so low only I could hear it. “I felt the first plan for that needle before the Hope-Binder was born. He has not got the physics right, by the way. The fourth harmonic is inverted. The thing will not unmake the Stasis. It will only sing for a moment and then swallow whatever holds it.” He paused. “They have worked so hard. It would be cruel to stop them now.”

I looked at him. The false mustache had slipped slightly, and I could see one corner of his neat beard beneath it. “What are you going to do?”

He did not answer. He was looking past me, across the crowd, and the crowd was beginning to notice something. I think it was the way the banners had stopped moving. The laws stitched into their cloth had frozen. The air in the great hollow had grown heavy, not with pressure but with a new kind of silence, as if the room were listening. One by one, the soldiers in the nearest rows turned toward the back where we stood. Somewhere behind the tier, a high, shrieking alarm began, and the Hope-Binder’s words died in his throat.

A young officer, her face a shifting cloud of white feathers, pointed at Godric. “The eyes,” she said. “The eyes.”

Godric had taken off the violet spectacles.

I will never forget the sound the Assembly made. It was not a battle cry. It was a single shared intake of breath, as if the whole redoubt had looked over the edge of the world and seen that there was no bottom. For four thousand years they had hidden. For one moment, they had believed. And now they saw him standing in their most sacred hall, wearing a straw hat and a false mustache, and the hope in them broke so quickly that it cracked the floor.

The Hope-Binder recovered first. He raised both arms, and the captured suns along his spine flared into furious life. “Begin the Final Verse!” he screamed. “Now! Do not wait for the appointed hour! Fire the needle!”

The resistance moved. It was a physical wave of preparation, a convulsion of arms and guns and maws and spells. The ceiling tore open, and above the nave, between the iron ribs of the fortress, I saw the weapon. It filled the upper dark like a second sea. It was a needle only in the way a galaxy is a pebble. Its body was a line of impossible white, thin and endless, and its point was not made of matter. It was made of every sacrifice they had burned for four thousand years, every world they had fed to the hidden engines, every hope-starved instant they had offered to the idea of killing Godric. The needle began to fall.

I did not run. I could not. The air had become a wall, and the wall was Godric’s patience. He stood with his hands still in the pockets of the brown coat. He did not raise them. He did not lower the hat. He did not even blink. The terrible mustache was still on his beard. He was, at that exact moment, the most absurd and most horrifying thing the omniverse has ever contained.

The needle struck him in the chest.

It did not touch his coat. It stopped a hair’s breadth from the fabric, not because a barrier caught it, but because the point had suddenly, completely, and finally understood what it was trying to pierce. The needle did not break. Breaking would have been a form of honor. It dissolved, from tip to tail, like a strand of salt dropped into an ocean that had no shore. The four thousand years of stored sacrifice poured out of it, but the energy did not explode. It turned to a warm, golden mist that gathered around Godric’s shoes and then faded into nothing, as if the whole effort had been a shy cloud offering him a pleasant stroll.

He turned to me. “I did not feel a tickle,” he said.

It was the mildness that ended the Assembly. Not his power. The words. They had spent four thousand years weaving a silence to hide from him, and the first thing he said was that their ultimate blow had not reached the surface of his attention. The Hope-Binder fell to his knees. The glass woman shattered into two hundred versions of herself and every version began to wail. The blind giant’s wheels spun and burned out, and the giant’s body sagged like a melting tower. The soldiers tried to run, and the floor became slow, and all around us the beautiful, hopeless city began to die.

What happened next was not an attack. Godric did not lift a hand. He did not let the terrible hat fall. Somewhere beneath the lowest root of his existence, the smallest, most restrained layer of a passive defense yet unfolded—not one of the sentient auras he keeps close, not one of the dreaming shields, but a microsecond of ambient awareness that had been waiting for the first hostile act to inconvenience him. That was all. A microsecond. The equivalent of a single eyelash turning toward a draft. The entire Final Liberty was erased from its own subcontinuum.

It was not a light. It was not a fire. The redoubt simply became no longer true. The iron city unwove from the inside out. The men and women and war-things were not thrown. They were not burned. They came apart into the smallest possible pieces of what they had been, and then those pieces came apart, and the sea above collapsed through the void where the fortress had hung. I saw the Hope-Binder try one last time to hold his shape, and his mouth opened around a word, and then his mouth was no longer a mouth but a smear of white heat moving backward through his own skull. The captured suns along his spine went out one by one, and each one made a sound like a child letting go of a rope. The city’s towers did not crumble. They leaned into themselves, as though each one had suddenly understood that it had always been a mistake. The entire hidden subcontinuum, with its dead time-shore and its swallowing sea and its thousands of years of frightened work, folded up into a single thin membrane, and the membrane tightened, and the membrane popped. I did not hear it. There was nothing left to hear. Only Godric, standing next to me on a bare, dark shore, adjusting his straw hat with both hands.

“I told you no one would believe it,” he said.

I did not know what I was supposed to say. My knees had gone soft, but I could still stand, because I had spent my whole life learning to stand near him. “The weapon,” I said at last. “It was the biggest resistance in the omniverse. It was supposed to erase the Stasis Event. And it did not even make you feel a tickle.”

He looked at me with genuine warmth, and his eyes were kind, the way they had always been kind. “No, Roth. It did not. It did not touch the smallest edge of the smallest shield. If I had allowed it to land on my skin, it would have been like one mote of dust trying to fight a supernova. If every one of them had built another four thousand years of weapons, and fired them all at once at the same point on the smallest dead cell of my body, the cell would not notice. That is not a boast. It is geometry. They were never close. They were not even in the same sentence as close.”

He took off the false mustache and tossed it into the dark. It vanished before it could drift. The violet spectacles went next, and then the hat, and when he turned back to me he was simply the King of Thronegate again, rugged and permanent and quietly pleased. The shore around us was empty. The sea had gone. The redoubt did not exist. There was only a long, soft darkness, and at the edge of it, the first pale light of the Thronegate star.

“I permitted them at first because I was curious,” he said. “They had a kind of doomed beauty, like a city built on the back of a whale that is already dying. And then I let them continue because they were the last. After this, no one will form a hostile thought against me for as long as existence persists. Not because I have broken their will. Their will is still their own. But because they have learned, all of them, that the idea of opposing me is less than the idea of a door in a wall that has no wall. It is not a choice anymore. It is a cat moving slowly away from a fire.”

I followed him into the pale light. The path opened again beneath our feet, not as a bridge, but simply as the way home. I did not speak for a long while. I could still see the Hope-Binder’s mouth opening around the last impossible word. I could still see the needle dissolving. And I kept hearing Godric’s voice, that warm, light, utterly normal voice, saying he had not felt a tickle. The rest of the omniverse had burned every last piece of itself to make a weapon, and he had not even taken his hands out of his pockets. That was the real horror, the one no journal could prepare you for. Not the death. The absence of effort. The absolute, unbroken ordinary calm of a man who had just let four thousand years of terror vanish without moving a muscle.

When we reached the courtyard again, the dried roses had not changed. The dead fountain waited. The palace lay golden in the late air. Godric stretched once, not like a man returning from battle, but like a man returning from a short walk to look at some interesting stones. He caught me watching him and smiled.

“I think I shall stop wearing mustaches,” he said. “You were right. It did not suit me.”

He turned toward the kitchens, still talking of whether the evening soup would be hot, and I followed him because there was no other direction. My heart was beating too fast and too slow at once. The largest resistance in omniversal history had died one day before its scheduled attack, and the only witness was a man who had worn a false mustache over his own immortal beard. He had let them prepare because they were the last, and now they were gone, and in their going they had proven the final truth of his rule. There was no outside to his patience. There was no moment in which a single hostile thought could survive his attention. He did not even need to turn his gaze toward them. He had been curious, and he had been amused, and then he had simply taken off a terrible disguise and let reality finish what their own fear had already started.

Later, I would write it down in the line of journals, because we all write it down. I would write that the Final Liberty had prepared for four thousand years, and that Godric had visited them one day before their attack, and that they had managed nothing, not a scratch, not a whisper, not a tickle. I would write that he had been friendly to me the whole time. That was the part the future wizards would not believe, and it was the part that would keep them awake. The cruelty was not in the annihilation. The cruelty was in the walk home, the soup, the warmth. The universe ended, and Godric wanted to know if the soup was hot. I did not tell him it was. I already knew it would be. It always was.
