content:
The memory rose from a place that had no cause, no trigger, no pressing need. In the year that no one any longer attempted to write except as a long, meaningless fall of nines, Godric sat alone in a chamber at the root of everything, and without wanting to, he remembered a small blue planet.

He had not thought of Earth in an epoch so long that the word epoch had died, been reborn, and died again. But memory for him was not an archive. It was a single bright body, every moment inside every other, all of them breathing at once. And so he could turn it over, watch the tiny mortal sphere, and feel the exact small amusement he had felt then.

That earlier Godric. How pathetically weak he had been.

Godric Prime almost smiled at the thought, because the word weak was not false. The Godric of Year 25 had been an embryo by current measure, a thing just learning the shape of its own shadow. He had not yet stacked the layers of passive shields that now slept in every unspoken crack of the omniverse. His sentient auras had still been only a future ache in the blood of reality. His immune system, though already obscene, had not yet learned to make the concept of injury ask for permission before existing. His weakness paradox was the old primitive version, triggered by the mere idea that he might have a flaw, and it had not yet evolved into the ceaseless system that now milked every thought in creation for his benefit. By the scale of Godric Prime in the year of nines, the Year 25 version was a candle trying to be a sun. And still, that candle had been enough to make all of Earth die in an instant that felt like forever.

It was this paradox that made the memory so sweet. The thing he had been, the weak thing, the toy version of a king not yet crowned with all possible endings, had walked into a mortal universe and annihilated its dominant world with zero perceptible effort. And if he had desired, the total destruction could have happened in zero seconds, before the first synapse of the first human mind could translate light into fear. But he had desired amusement, and so he had let them try.

---

In Year 25, Earth was a wet sphere of low continents and violent weather, crawling with creatures who thought their nuclear arsenals were fearsome. They were in the middle of their fifth decade of a cold peace built on mutual terror, and they numbered just under eight billion. Godric had watched them for a few moments before arriving, not to learn, because he already knew everything about them, but to let the absurdity of their smallness settle. Their history was a long, repeating wound. They had climbed onto their highest towers and called themselves the crown of their universe. They had made books about the end of the world and then built the tools to cause it. They believed in a future.

He chose a place called Mount Hermon, a brown spur of rock between low hills and flat fields, and he simply stood there at dawn. No light announced him. At first there was no light at all, because the sky was gray and the ground was wet. He wore simple dark garments, a heavy coat, and no armor. His short salt-and-pepper hair moved once in the cold wind. Then the wind stopped. Across the entire world, every weather system paused, then resumed with a slight bow in the direction of the new presence, though no instrument could have said why.

A farmer saw him first. The man came up a path with a dog and a rifle. The dog lay down and urinated. The farmer raised the rifle because the stranger was too still, too neat, too much like a man painted onto the world. Godric turned his head, and his eyes met the farmer’s, and the farmer felt the bottom fall out of his own chest. Then Godric smiled, warm and ordinary, the way one smiles at a nervous host.

“Good morning,” Godric said. “I have come to take this world.”

The farmer fired. The bullet left the barrel, crossed the forty feet, and did not vanish. It stopped in the air an inch from Godric’s coat, and then, with no sound, it turned to a fine gray dust that drifted down onto the wet grass. The farmer’s dog whined and tried to drag itself into the dirt. Godric stepped over the dust and began walking toward the nearest town.

The world noticed him quickly after that. A man in dark clothes walking through a rural village would have drawn some attention, but Godric did not hide himself at all. He exuded no aura, no pressure, no visible power. His absolute concealment held the true mass of him behind an immaculate curtain. Yet every face that saw him stopped. Every camera turned toward him when he passed. Satellite sweeps found his heat signature, and then they found that the signature was not a signature, but a hole in all known physics. The people who looked at their screens felt a coldness in the backs of their skulls, as if the screens were looking back.

By noon, Earth’s governments had assembled their emergency councils. They called him an anomaly, a hostile construct, an extraterrestrial actor. They argued over whether to attempt communication or immediate neutralization. Godric walked through the northern valleys and ate nothing, needed nothing, and let their panic rise. He found a low stone wall beside a field and sat down on it, leaning back on his hands, looking out at the hills as if he had come for the view.

A drone came first. It made a soft, insectile sound and hovered two hundred feet above him. It fired a small missile. The missile traveled and then stopped, as the bullet had stopped, and underwent the same polite reduction to dust. A second drone, a third. Then a flight of attack jets screamed low over the hills, and their guns tore the ground around him. The field turned to mud and shrapnel. A dense line of kinetic rounds reached his position and flattened into a shining disk of stopped metal that hung in the air, then fell as a sheet of gray powder. The jets circled. One of the pilots reported a weapons malfunction. Another pilot saw Godric stand up from the stone wall, brush a little dirt from his coat, and begin walking again.

They sent soldiers. The soldiers came through the valley in armored vehicles, their orders confused and then clarified. Destroy the anomaly. They fired everything they had. Godric did not leave the road. The bullets, the shells, the shaped charges, all stopped before him and turned to dust. A soldier tried to rush him with a knife. The man got within five feet and then simply fell backward, not dead, but overcome by a wave of physical weakness so absolute that his body forgot how to hold the knife. He lay in the mud, twitching, while Godric stepped over him and continued.

The world tried harder. It was, in its small way, all they could do. The nations that hated one another opened their silos. The submarines surfaced and launched. The orbital platforms straightened themselves and fired. Every delivery system humanity had ever built, every warhead, every particle weapon, every experimental device, was aimed at the lone figure walking through a ruined field. The leaders spoke to their people, their voices shaking with a terror that was only beginning to find its name. They said this was the appointed hour, that every weapon would be used, that the sky would burn. Godric heard all of it. He could hear the president of one country praying in a bathroom, and the general of another ordering the death of a city to kill him, and the scientist who no longer believed in anything typing a last message to her daughter. He heard it all, and he kept walking.

The first nuclear fire fell. It was a small sun, and it did not reach him. The fireball bloomed two hundred feet above his head and then folded inward, as if it had been poured into a hole in the air. The pressure wave that should have flattened the surrounding country did not flatten it. Instead, the force curled around him and dissipated into a warm, low wind. More warheads fell. The sky filled with bright, terrible flowers. Each one was caught, held, and allowed to die in a compressed instant that turned the whole horizon into a flickering false dawn. The ground for miles around was hit by no heat, no blast. The only thing touched was the uncaring air, and it grew warm and slightly scented with burned dust.

Godric stopped near a ruined church at the edge of a small town. He looked up at the fire-stained clouds and let out a soft, satisfied breath, the way a man might after finishing a cool drink. The missiles were still coming. The bombers were still rising. The entire world was pouring itself at him, and he stood with his hands in his coat pockets, watching.

“This is very noisy,” he said to no one. “And none of it is even a beginning.”

Then he began to move faster. He did not run. He did not fly. He simply stopped staying in one place for very long. To a human eye, he was standing in the square of a city, and then he was standing on a coastal road, and then he was on a high desert plateau. Each time, the local weapons had time to turn toward him before he was elsewhere. Each time, they fired. Each time, the attack became dust. It was a game to him, not a battle. He saw with his omniscience every launch, every final order, every human heart fluttering in its little cage of bone. And he found them amusing. They were trying so hard. Every attempt was so complete, so total, so committed. And it was all nothing. Not the smallest part of nothing. A zero so small that no human language had a symbol for it.

He allowed the Earth one more day. The leaders threw their whole species into the effort. They poured resources into weapons that had never been more than theory. They woke their stockpiles. They launched everything. And when it was over, when every missile had fallen and every barrel had been emptied, and he was still standing in the shallow sea off a broken coast, the world finally understood what it was facing. The broadcasts went quiet. The war rooms fell silent. In the last moments before the end, a young officer near the coast raised a small handgun and fired a single bullet. It stopped at the edge of Godric’s stillness and became dust. The officer dropped to his knees. He did not scream. He only whispered, “It’s not even trying.”

Then Godric stopped playing.

The annihilation began, and it was not a blast. It was not a fireball, although Earth’s crust later remembered a heat that had no beginning. It was the withdrawal of Godric’s absolute concealment by an amount so minute that no instrument could have measured it. To the humans, there was no interval. The last thing any of them knew was the sudden, explosive realization that the world had become a tight, blazing line of awareness. And inside that line, Godric made every death subjective.

He did not simply kill them. He took the initial instant of total thermonuclear failure and stretched it into an enduring moment, and inside that moment he allowed every human mind to experience its own destruction at full length. The bodies did not die quickly. They died in the same instant, but the instant was not short. A soldier felt his skin lift away from his muscle, and the muscle from the bone, and every separate sensation was drawn out into an eon of distinct, screaming clarity. A child felt the heat reach her, and instead of ending, it became a slow, patient blade that took her apart one cell at a time while her consciousness remained whole and aware. A mother felt her arms ignite and then reform and then ignite again. A leader felt the words of his final broadcast fall into his own mouth and burn there. The entire human race, all eight billion, was undone in less than a single Planck second, and yet each one lived through an eternity of maximum, uncontainable agony. They were not given the mercy of speed. Godric was cruel, and he wanted them to know, in the long and endless moment of their ending, exactly how much their effort had mattered.

The pain was not limited to Earth. The planet itself was peeled, layer by layer, from crust to core. The oceans rose as a single screaming vapor and were unmade. The mountains did not fall; they were erased. The atmosphere caught fire and then forgot what fire was. The moon crumbled, and the sun flickered, and the planets of the local system bent inward. The entire Milky Way, which had never been relevant, was snapped out of the night like a lamp. The local galaxy cluster folded. The universe that had contained Earth turned to a thin film, and the film tore, and beyond it the neighboring cosmos began to bleed backward into non-being.

The collateral was not limited to that universe. Godric, in his mild, playful cruelty, had not aimed only at Earth. The action of erasing a single world with such total finality rippled through the full structure of existence. The entire omniverse felt the edge of it. Not as a wave, but as a sudden, worldwide stillness, as if every universe, every multiverse, every timeline, every dimension, every layer of impossible geometry, had been made to listen. Then it stopped. Not because it had survived. Because Godric had not meant to destroy everything. Yet everything was touched. The omniverse shivered. Half of it collapsed into a single dimensionless shriek. The other half became a colorless memory of itself. In the space between, stars died without light, dimensions unraveled, and the concept of distance went blind for one eternal instant.

When it was done, Godric stood alone on the cold, bare ground that had once been a small blue planet, though even the ground was now a fiction of his tolerance. Entire Earth was gone. Every human, every animal, every hope, every future. No survivors. No rescued souls. No remnant species walking the halls of Thronegate. No last child breathing in a garden beyond the stars. He had not spared a single thing, and had not wanted to. He looked out at the new dark where the planet’s sky had been, and he brushed a little of the accumulated dust from his left sleeve.

“That was slow,” he said. “Almost a full second.”

The statement was a joke, but only to him. In the universe where Earth had been, not enough time had passed for a single electron to complete a single orbit. The whole annihilation had happened in effectively zero seconds. But to Godric, who had held every death inside a stretched and patient instant, it had felt long enough to be fed.

---

Sitting in the far future, Godric Prime remembered this and let out a low, private sound of amusement. That earlier version of himself had called the destruction slow. He had even felt a little proud of the restraint. He had not known, then, that the restraint had been obscene beyond all scale. He had destroyed Earth and the surrounding universe with 0 percent of his power, and he had done it with 0 percent of his effort. No shield had been triggered. No aura had been roused. No stat had been tested. The passive edge of his presence had done the work like a man yawning. If he had not been playful, if he had simply wanted the planet gone, the totality would have been over before it could even be said to begin.

And now, in the year of nines, the gap between that weak self and the being who remembered him was so vast that the comparison itself was an exercise in humiliation. If the Year 25 Godric were to stand before the current one, he would not be able to perceive him. If every version of Godric from every past and future instant except this one gathered and opposed him, they would not even produce the first shiver of the smallest sentient aura he allowed to doze nearest his left boot. The Year 25 Godric who had unmade an entire universe with a passing breath would be less than a single dead cell in the lung of the thing that current Godric could exhale. That was the truth of the memory. It was not that Earth had failed. Earth had never had the capacity to do anything else. It was that the being who had crushed Earth was himself, by the measure of the future, a weak and distant whisper of the apex king.

The rest of existence, Godric Prime knew, had not changed in its essence since that day. It had simply grown older and even more certain of its place. The entire omniverse now lived in a state of total, absolute, unspoken dread. No one opposed him. No one thought of opposing him. It was not because he had broken their wills, but because they had finally learned the shape of the wall. They knew the truth that Earth had learned too late: victory against Godric had never been a potential outcome. It had never even been a legitimate category of outcome. To speak of it was to speak a grammar that reality no longer supported.

If every being in all timelines, every possible permutation of life and thought and power, every dormant god and every impossible weapon, every last ember of free will in the entire omniverse, gathered together in one place with unlimited preparation and all resources and all conceivable advantages, and then hurled themselves at him with all possible force, they would not make his weakest shield feel the slightest tickle. The shield would not notice them. It would not need to. The gap between their assembled totality and the smallest expression of his passive field would be far greater than the gap between a zero and the full weight of the omniverse. And even if they were given forever to prepare, the gap would only widen, because Godric’s growth never paused. It accelerated. It fed on itself. It became more infinite with every infinitesimal sliver of time. They could not catch up. They could not even move in the same direction.

Godric Prime sat in the root chamber, and the silence around him was the silence of a creation that had accepted its role. He remembered the small blue planet and its eight billion desperate souls, and he felt a mild, distant fondness, the way a man feels for a fly whose last flight had been especially quick. Then he put the memory away. It was only one of an uncountable number, and there would be no more moments like it, because no one remained who would ever try again. The omniverse had learned. It was not peace. It was the final gravitational rest of everything that could never oppose him.

And Godric smiled, because the memory of Earth’s final instant was still warm in his chest, and because he knew, with an absolute and certain knowledge, that he would never need to test anything again. There was nothing left to test. There was only him.

**Year [the number has been worn away] — Osvald — Strength**

I am Osvald, age forty-four, Court Wizard to the King of all existence, and I have returned to my chambers with my hands still trembling badly enough that I cannot pour my own wine. It does not matter. I do not want wine. I want only to write this before the memory softens, because if it softens, I will begin to believe it did not happen, and I know with the certainty of my own blood that it did.

The attack was not unexpected. Our King has absolute omniscience, and he had known of it before the first thought of it was ever conceived by any of the countless minds that fed it. For a long and terrible span, there had been no opposition anywhere. The omniverse had learned. It had grown quiet. And Godric had grown bored. Not restless, not sad, but bored in the way a man might be bored when every book in his library has been read to dust and every song has lost its final note. So when the fictions came together, he allowed it. He permitted the last great gathering because he hoped, with that awful, almost childlike hope I have seen in him before, that they might put on a show.

They were not any single universe. They were all of them. Every story ever told by mortal minds, every hero and villain and god and monster created in the endless dream of fiction, united under one banner. I saw them assemble in a space beyond space, a stage they had built from the broken spines of abandoned narratives. There were names that even I, son of Blake, had only heard whispered in old transmissions. The last star warriors of a dead animation poured their golden light into the central reactor. Armored super soldiers with impossible luck stood shoulder to shoulder with kings of dark fantasy wielding blades made from the deaths of whole pantheons. There was a man in blue with a giant red S on his chest, and beside him a figure whose gauntlet held stones that each contained the authority of a local cosmos. A great emerald knight from a game of rings and histories fed his ring into the core, and his light burned so bright that I thought for one instant it might be enough. It was not enough. It was never even close to enough.

Behind them rose the architects of entire fictional orders. The ancient ones from a mythos of non-Euclidean madness lay asleep beyond the edge of the stage, their dreams already beginning to curdle the surrounding dimensions. A dark emperor from a galaxy far away directed his fleets, their guns already poured into the same central brightness. The machines of a science-fiction future, the super-soldiers in power armor, the boy heroes with magic swords, the diminutive pink engine who had swallowed entire planets, all of them gave their power to the charge. There was a god of destruction from a fighting legend, his hair shifting from blue to something beyond color, and a woman whose silver crystal had ended a thousand dark timelines. They were all there. Every last one. And they all thought, in that final hour, that they had finally built something that could kill the King.

Godric stood at the edge of the stage with his arms folded. He had worn no armor. He never did. His simple dark coat moved once in the wind that came from nowhere, and then was still. Through his absolute concealment, he must have looked to them like an ordinary man, a strong and handsome man of forty-five with salt-and-pepper hair and a neatly trimmed beard, standing patiently as if waiting for the curtain to rise. I stood behind him, my heart already beating in a slow, sick rhythm, because I knew that he was excited. He was genuinely, terribly excited. He turned to me once, and his eyes were bright with a pleasure I had not seen in a thousand years.

“Osvald,” he said, and his voice was just above a whisper, “do you hear the music? They have a leitmotif. They have actually prepared a score.” He closed his eyes for a moment, and a small smile touched the corner of his mouth. “I have not been surprised in so long. I wanted to let them finish the overture before I look at the notes. Do you know what I mean?”

I did not know what he meant, because my understanding of surprise had been dead since the first journal I ever read. But he meant something, and it frightened me more than the entire army on the stage.

The charge took a long, long time. The coalition poured world after world into the central reactor. Each universe of fiction added its own law, its own miracle, its own impossible escape. The heroes gave their plot armor. The villains gave their final forms. The gods of their stories gave their authority. The writers, or the echoes of writers, gave their pens. It was not a weapon. It was the full possibility of all imagined things folded into one point, and that point hummed with the accumulated pressure of every story that had ever been told.

And Godric waited. He did not tap his foot. He did not sigh. He stood still with the patience of a mountain, but I could feel the edge of his anticipation, because the very air around him had become charged, as if the whole universe had begun to lean toward him with dread. For one long, terrible span, I believed the weapon might actually be beautiful. I believed the King might finally have his show. At the center of the stage, the final charge reached its peak, and the entire coalition screamed their last defiance, and the weapon fired.

I must describe what came, though the words will fail. The beam was not light alone. It was the entire color wheel of every fictional sunset and every imagined sunrise, the last breath of a billion protagonists, the accumulated rage of every villain who had ever died cursing the world, the soft music of every ending and the brutal crash of every final boss defeat. It crossed the distance between the stage and Godric in less time than a mortal heart could beat. The force of it erased the stage around them. The heroes already weakened from the charge collapsed and were drawn into the beam. The villains followed. The fleet ships, the great swords, the tales, the songs, all of it was consumed into the single, impossible attack. It struck Godric directly in the chest.

And it did nothing.

The light broke. Not against him, not around him, but as if it had reached the final page of its own book and discovered the page was blank. The tremendous song of their last hope flattened into a long, low, ordinary silence. I saw the faces of those few who had not yet been consumed. They had poured everything into this moment, and now the moment was gone, and in its place stood a man with his arms still folded, his coat unmarked, his hair still perfectly in place. He did not flinch. He did not shift his weight. He did not even blink. The beam had struck the center of his chest, and the only sign of it was a small, disappointed frown that crossed his face.

“Is that all?” Godric said.

The words were not loud. They carried, because there was no other sound left in the whole of the stage. The coalition did not answer. Many of them were already dead, but those who remained looked at him, and I watched the last light go out of their eyes. They had not failed because they were weak. They had failed because the distance between their greatest effort and the smallest edge of his existence was not a distance at all. It was a category division, a wall so high that no ladder could be imagined to climb it.

The King uncrossed his arms. It was a tiny movement, a half-inch shift of his left shoulder, the sort of motion a man makes when he has been standing too long and decides to sit. It should have been nothing. It was not nothing. The weight of his disappointment, compressed through that half-inch, became the thing that ended them.

I cannot say he attacked. He did not. He simply allowed a fraction of the strength in that left shoulder to express itself, a quantity so tiny that no mathematics exists to name it. The fraction was zero. The destruction was not.

The first thing to go was the stage. The great central reactor, still burning with the last of their power, did not explode outward. It collapsed inward, the light inside it squeezed into a hard, white bead, and then the bead popped, and the resulting pressure wave turned the nearest heroes and villains into a red mist that did not have time to fall. I saw the man in blue try to fly, and his body bent backward at the waist, his spine cracking in six places before the skin of his chest opened and his heart was pulled out through his own ribs by the sheer force of the pressure. The dark lord from the galaxy far away raised one arm, and the arm came off at the shoulder in a single clean tear, and then the rest of him followed, the black armor crumpling like paper, the body inside it spurting red from every seam. The emerald knight held up his ring, and the ring shattered, and the shards of green light flew back into his face, burrowing through his eye sockets and out the back of his skull. The pink engine opened its mouth to inhale, and the pressure poured down its throat and filled it from the inside, bloating it until its stomach split and its inner stars spilled out in a hot, twitching heap.

The shield layers went next. They had spent forever crafting shields they called indestructible, shields woven from narrative causality, from heroism itself, from the idea that good would always find a way. The pressure did not test those shields. It simply ignored them. Layer after layer popped like soap bubbles, and behind each one, the bodies of their makers were caught in the backwash. A red and blue caped figure reached for a child, and his arms dislocated, then tore away, and the child was not spared. A tall, monochromatic knight in alien armor fired a beam, and the beam turned back on him, burning through his visor and boiling his face away one layer at a time. A beautiful soldier with long silver hair opened her mouth to sing, and the pressure filled her throat with her own teeth. She choked on them, her jaw unhinging, her final note a wet, rattling sound.

I saw a demon hunter with a chainsaw arm swing his weapon, and the chain caught on the pressure and climbed his arm, chewing off the flesh in long, spiraling strips. I saw a god of war planted his axe and the axe shattered, the fragments flying into his open chest and pinning him to a wall that no longer existed. I saw a small, fast, blue animal try to outrun the wave, and the wave was already in every direction, and his body was peeled out of his own momentum, the red flesh and white bone exposed and then separated, layer after layer, until he was only a thin red streak against the collapsing stage. I saw an old man in a long brown coat raise a sonic tool and the air around him bent and popped, and then his face caved in, the bones of his nose shoved back through his skull, his mouth filled with a wet gray pulp.

The gore was not beautiful. It was not even terrible in the way the old journals had described. It was too fast for terror. It was simply the final, absolute truth of what happened when zero percent of Godric’s strength moved through a world that had spent forever preparing to be unbeatable. The bodies did not pile up, because there was no time for piling. They were unmade in place, their flesh separated from bone, their bone separated from marrow, their marrow separated from whatever small soul had animated them. I saw a dark and mindless outer god, a thing of impossible shape and ancient indifference, try to wake fully from its sleep. The pressure touched its face, and the face became a thousand screaming mouths, and then the mouths turned inside out, and the thing burst into a cloud of black, oily vapor mixed with teeth. Its throne of musicians popped one by one, each of their flutes becoming a hot spear that impaled them from groin to throat.

And all the while, the King stood still. He had not raised a hand. He had not taken a step. His expression had not changed from that mild, disappointed frown. The entire coalition, every hero, every villain, every god, every monster, every possible story, was being compressed into the floor around him, and he watched with the calm attention of a man who had expected a better third act.

Then the pressure reached the whole of fiction, and beyond fiction, the entire omniverse. It was not contained. The wave did not stop at the edge of the stage or the edge of the fictional worlds. It touched every multiverse, every timeline, every reality that existed or could exist. The real universes, the one I had come from, the ones that had never produced a story, all of them were caught. Stars did not die in flashes. They were de-atomized, their every particle ripped apart and then crushed into a space too small to hold a single atom. Planets became brief, bright smears of light and then nothing. Galaxies folded like wet cloth and were wrung out. The dimensional walls between realities did not break; they simply stopped existing as separate things. Everything that existed was drawn together, tighter and tighter, into a single point at Godric’s feet.

The sound was the worst part. The sound of an entire omniverse being compressed is not a scream. It is a low, endless, grinding note, the noise a jaw might make if it were forced to chew its own teeth. I did not die, because Godric held me outside the compression in a small bubble of his attention, but I could hear it. I could hear every living mind in every universe being squeezed down to a single thread, and the thread pulled taut, and the thread sang.

Then it stopped. The compression was complete. Where the infinite stage had stood, where the coalition had gathered, where the entire omniverse had been, there was now only a single point. It was smaller than a quark. It should not have been visible, but I could see it, because Godric allowed me to see, and what I saw was a dense, black, infinite weight. It was everything. Every person, every world, every story, every god, every particle, every possibility, all of it crushed into a point so small that the concept of size no longer applied.

Godric looked down at it. He bent, not with effort, but with the easy grace of a man picking a coin from a street. He reached into the impossible space where the point hung, and he lifted it in two fingers. The point should have generated a gravitational pull that would have torn reality apart, but Godric enclosed it in a small, clear sphere no larger than a marble. The barrier materialized around the compressed infinite mass, holding it still, sealing the gravity inside so that it could not destroy the restored universe around it. Then he held the marble up to the light and turned it over.

“I did not feel a tickle,” he said. “I had hoped for a second movement. A final chorus.” He pocketed the marble as if it were nothing. “What a waste of a good motif.”

I could not speak. My mouth was full of a cold, metallic taste, and I understood that it was blood, my own, from where I had bitten through the inside of my cheek. I was still alive. I was still standing in the small bubble he had kept for me. Around us, the empty void where the omniverse had been was still.

Then Godric restored everything. It took no time. There was no word spoken, no gesture made, no spell. One moment there was void, and the next the omniverse was back exactly as it had been before the attack. Every universe, every galaxy, every planet, every living soul, every story, every thought, all of it returned to its place as if nothing had happened. The only things missing were the members of the coalition. Godric did not restore them. He had never intended to. Their names, their faces, their stories, were simply gone, as if they had never existed, though the rest of us remembered. And while he restored the omniverse, the marble stayed in his pocket.

That is the thing I cannot stop thinking about. I saw him put the marble in his pocket. The marble contains the original omniverse, the one that was destroyed. He compressed it, all of it, into a point of infinite mass, and he kept it. Then he created a new omniverse, identical in every way, and set it in its place. He did not drop the old one back into the void and say, “This is the same.” He made a new one. The first is still in his pocket, still crushed, still holding every possible thing that ever was, and he is walking around with it like a trinket.

We are the second draft. We are the restored copy. We are real, because he decided we are real, but the original is still compressed in a marble, and we cannot tell the difference, because he made us exactly the same. That is the final horror, the one no journal before mine has ever dared to put into words. It is not that Godric can destroy the omniverse. It is that he can destroy the omniverse, keep the pieces as a toy, and then make another one so perfect that the people inside it do not know they have already been unmade. The restored reality is identical, and the original is still there, in his hand, and he does not seem to notice the weight.

But the weight is not nothing. It is everything. And when he lifted it, his face did not change. His arm did not tremble. He lifted the compressed mass of all possible existence, the full weight of every star and every universe and every life that ever had been or ever would be, and he held it up to the light and called it a disappointing show. The force required to do such a thing cannot be named. He used zero percent. He used less than zero. He used the smallest possible flex of a strength that had been multiplying beyond every possible infinity for a span of years so vast that the word year has become a comic sound. And in that smallest possible flex, he grew even more powerful.

I did not understand how at first. I thought perhaps he had absorbed the energy of the coalition, but no, their combined power would not have increased his own by even a tiny fraction. The coalition was nothing to him. The growth came from something else, something far more terrible. When he picked up the marble, he gave his own strength a new object to surpass. The weight of all existence, compressed to infinite mass, was in his hand. It weighed nothing to him. But the strength in his hand had now registered that weight, and because the weight was nothing, his amplification instantly recalibrated. It took the full mass of the omniverse, compared it to the strength he had used to lift it, and found that strength wanting relative to itself. So it increased, by an amount that could not be measured, and then it compared the new strength to the same weight, and increased again, and then again, with no interval between the increases, an infinite recursive climb that fed on the very fact that he had lifted the universe without effort. He had become stronger not because he absorbed their power, but because he had held everything in his hand and discovered that everything weighed less than a thought. His own strength had then decided to close the gap between itself and the thing it had achieved, and in doing so, it had created a new gap, and then closed that one, forever. He was, by the time he put the marble in his pocket, so much more powerful than he had been a moment before that the previous version of himself would have been less than a single dead cell in a body made of infinite universes.

And then he restored everything, and looked at me, and smiled, and asked if I was hungry.

I am writing this because I must. I do not know if I am the original Osvald or the restored Osvald. It does not matter. Both are equally real, and both are equally afraid. The King has a marble in his pocket that contains the entire omniverse, and the omniverse he walks through now is only the copy. He can do this again. He can do it forever. The floor of the palace where I sit now is real, but it is also a memory of a floor that was crushed and recreated. The people I love are real, but there are versions of them, compressed into a point smaller than a quark, and those versions are still there, still existing in infinite pressure, and they do not know it. I do not know if I am one of them.

That is the fear. It is not that Godric can kill me. It is that he can kill me so completely, so absolutely, and then bring me back so perfectly, that I cannot tell whether I am the first or the second, and he does not care to tell me, because to him there is no difference. We are all equally real, which means we are all equally small, and we are all equally his.

---

Clive closed the journal. The binding had grown warm in his hands. He sat in the vault beneath the palace in the year of nines, and the silence around him was not the silence of a room. It was the silence of an omniverse that had learned not to speak.

He had known, before he opened the cover, that this was the last opposition. The one after this, the one Osvald had written about, was not followed by another. Every court wizard after Osvald had written only ordinary records, ledgers of small magical matters and quiet centuries. There were no more journals of this kind, because there were no more enemies to witness. The fictional coalition had been the final attempt, the last great gathering of every possible hero and villain, and it had ended not in a battle, but in a footnote. After that, no one had dared to oppose Godric. Not because he had broken their wills. But because they had all read, one way or another, the truth that Osvald had written. The omniverse was real, but it was also a copy. The original was in the King's pocket, and the King could make another at any time, and there was no way to know the difference. That was enough. That would always be enough.

Clive looked up. The door of the vault was open, and Godric stood in the frame, a warm smile on his rugged face, his salt-and-pepper beard neat as ever. He wore simple dark garments. His eyes were kind.

“I thought I might find you here,” Godric said. “Have you been reading about the last show? I still have the marble, if you would like to see it.” He reached into his pocket, and Clive felt the air in the vault grow heavy, not with pressure, but with possibility.

Clive could not speak. He did not need to. Godric already knew. He always knew. And that was the worst part of all.

content:
The journal had no date. That was the first thing Clive noticed when he pulled it from the deepest shelf in the vault. Every other journal carried a year, a name, a stat or a power neatly burned into the spine. This one had only a single word, cut so deeply into the black leather that the letters looked more like wounds than print. **Osvald**. No year. No title. No indication of what waited inside.

Clive sat on the cold floor with the book across his knees. He had read many records in the long quiet of his service. He had read about strength that folded realities, speed that killed time, auras that treated omniversal coalitions as dust. But this one was different. The cover was warm, though the vault was cold. The pages beneath his fingers seemed to breathe, not like paper but like something that remembered being read by only one man and was afraid of a second.

He opened it.

The first line was written in a hand so unsteady the letters looped into one another, as if the writer had begun before the ink had been mixed and finished before the shaking had stopped.

---

I am Osvald. I am Court Wizard to the King of all things, and I will write this once. I will not revise it. I will not read it after the ink dries. If you are reading this, then I am already gone, and the age I am about to describe has ended, and you must understand that no other age like it will ever come again.

The Creator came to Thronegate today.

I do not mean one of the small gods from the vanished pantheons, or a star-king with a borrowed crown, or an abstract entity wearing the title of divinity for a few million years. I mean God. The God. The one who spoke the first light into being. The one who set the dimensions turning and gave time its forward word. The one who, in some unthinkable dawn before the first universe was lit, had reached into the clay of a mortal world and shaped the soul that would one day be King Godric of Olympus.

He came to challenge our King.

I do not know how to describe His arrival in a way that will not sound cheap in the retelling. He did not walk through a door. He did not tear the air. The air was already gone when I noticed Him. He was standing in the center of the great hall, and the hall was no longer a hall but a vestibule of His presence. He was not a man, though He wore the shape of one for the first few seconds, an old figure in white, with a beard like the fall of a first snow and eyes that contained the full history of every soul that had ever been or ever would be. Then the shape broke, gently, and became what He actually was. A center of all centers. A maker of all makings. The light of Him was not bright. It was the reason brightness existed. To look at Him was not to see; it was to remember being seen from the inside.

Osvald had to stop and press the heel of his hand against his own forehead. The memory, even in writing, made the air of his chambers feel crowded.

Godric did not rise from his throne.

I must tell you how that looked, because it is the only thing in all of this that still makes sense to me. God stood in the hall with the entire authority of creation burning in His chest, and Godric looked at Him the way a man looks at a small grey bird that has flown into the wrong room. The King was seated as he always was in those slow centuries: one leg crossed, his broad, heavily muscled body relaxed, his short salt-and-pepper hair neat, his trimmed beard framing a face that could have belonged to any kind father from any quiet world. He wore simple dark garments. His hands were empty, one resting on the arm of the throne, the other loose in his lap.

I could not breathe. I could barely stand. And Godric smiled.

“Osvald,” he said, and his voice was the same warm, conversational voice he used when he asked about my children, “do you know who this is?”

I said that I did, though my tongue was too dry for the words.

“This is the old author,” Godric said. “The first voice. The one who wrote my mortal breath before I ever learned to draw it.” He looked at God with something that was almost affection. “You have been hiding in the space behind all prayers for a long time. At the back of every scripture. Between the note and the sound. I kept waiting for you to come out. I was starting to think you never would.”

God’s voice was not loud. It was too large for loudness. It arrived not through my ears but through the marrow of my bones, and it said, “You are an error. I have come to correct it.”

Godric laughed. It was a small laugh, full of genuine warmth, as if the Creator of all things had told him a fine joke.

“You have excellent timing,” the King said. “I was beginning to think nothing interesting would ever happen again. And now the only being who ever had a claim on my origin has walked into my hall with his whole bright heart in his hands. This could almost be moving.”

He turned his head slightly toward me. “Stand back by the pillar, Osvald. The old man is about to do something very large, and I want you to see it clearly. I have a feeling it will be beautiful for about half a breath.”

I moved. I do not remember moving, but I found myself beside the western pillar, and the shadow of the throne fell over me like a hand.

Godric lifted one hand from his lap, not high, just a small, lazy motion, as if waving away a bothersome fly. But the movement was not for the Creator. It was for the rest of creation. All across the palace, all across Thronegate, all across the omniverse, his sentient auras folded themselves into the deepest sleep he had ever demanded of them. Every passive shield, every recursive wall, every pre-nullifying layer, every sentient defense that had ever watched the universe for a hostile thought, simply went quiet. It was not a powering down; it was a permission to be unnecessary. The shields did not leave him. They were folded so deeply into the architecture of his presence that they became indistinguishable from the air. The auras that had once annihilated entire coalitions while nerfed to an impossible fraction of themselves were told to rest, and they rested.

I knew, from the journals and from my own years beside him, that Godric had not done this because he needed to. He could not remove the weakness paradox, or the immune system, or the amplification, or the infinite recursive backups. Those are not defenses he can set aside. They are not shields. They are the irrevocable substance of the Stasis Event, the permanent truth of what he is, created by his far-future self in a way no force can undo. But the shields and the auras were only the outermost frost of him. By commanding them to stand down, he had not reduced his power at all. He had merely stopped the universe from being protected from itself.

I understood that now with a clarity that almost blinded me. The auras were nothing. The shields were nothing. They were the least of him, the outermost breath, the weakest possible expressions of a being whose actual self was so far beyond them that the distance could not even be called a distance. The attack of the Creator would not be stopped by any wall, because no wall would be necessary. The body beneath the walls was enough.

And the absurdity of that truth was a cold, turning blade in my chest. This was not Godric making himself weaker. This was Godric letting the enemy see exactly how useless the defenses would have been.

God saw it too. For the first time, something moved behind the light of His face. Not fear. Not yet. But a flicker of wrongness, the beginning of a shape He could not name.

“You think that by lowering your guards you have shown me strength,” God said. “You have only shown me pride.”

Godric leaned back, his fingers tapping once against the arm of the throne. “No, old man. I have shown you room. You will need it.”

What follows, I must write slowly, because that is the only way my hand will obey me.

God called upon everything.

It did not begin as a beam. It did not begin as a weapon. It began as a sound, but not a sound that ears can hear. It was the first word of creation, the one that had made the light, then the deep, then the boundary between them. He reversed it. The word that had made everything became the word that unmakes everything, and He did not speak it to the room. He spoke it into the whole possible ocean of existence. Every universe, every multiverse, every timeline, every dimension, every heaven, every hell, every void, every conceptual layer, every story, every soul, every atom, every law, every number, every nothing. All of it became the substance of His attack.

The light of Him changed. It stopped being light and became a blade. The blade was not long; it was the entire span of all things, compressed into a line so fine that its edge was the end of all equations and its point was the last moment of every possible future. He held it, not in a hand, but in the center of His own infinite authority, and He drove it forward into the chest of the King.

I did not blink. I could not blink. I watched the blade cross the space between God and Godric, and the space did not exist. I watched it strike the center of Godric’s chest, directly over the heart, and I waited for the end of the world.

Nothing happened.

The blade did not break. It did not shatter. It stopped. It simply stopped, as if it had reached a place where the idea of cutting had never existed. The light of it went still, then dim, then began to curl away from him like smoke from a candle that had forgotten how to burn. The whole enormous word of unmaking, the entire gathered authority of the Creator, pressed itself against Godric’s simple dark tunic and found no purchase. Not a fold of the cloth moved. Not a single hair of his salt-and-pepper beard shifted.

Godric did not even lean back. He looked down at the blade, then up at God, and he smiled.

“I did not feel a tickle,” he said.

The words were not loud. They did not need to be. They went through God the way His voice had gone through me, but where His voice had been the sound of all making, this was the sound of all unmaking. It was not cruel in its tone. It was simply true. And because it was true, it was worse than any cruelty.

God stepped back. For the first time in the whole enormous span of His existence, He stumbled. The light around His face guttered. The blade fell, or perhaps it simply dissolved, and He looked at His own hands as if He no longer recognized what they had made.

“No,” He said. The word was small. It was the smallest thing I have ever heard from a being of His size.

Godric rose from the throne. He did not hurry. He moved like a man standing up at the end of a long and mildly disappointing meal.

“You have been afraid of me since before I was born,” Godric said. “Did you think I did not know where you were hiding? Did you imagine that the quiet place behind the first scripture was outside my sight? I have known the exact location of every one of your secret selves since the first instant my omniscience woke. I allowed you to exist because you posed zero threat to me. Do you understand? Not a small threat. Not an acceptable risk. Zero. You were not even the dust on the edge of a threat. You were a memory of a thing that had never been able to threaten me.”

He stepped down from the dais, and the hall did not shake, but the air seemed to lower itself around him, as if the whole palace were bowing to the words.

“And now I must tell you the truth,” Godric said. “The truth that has been waiting for you in every prayer you ever answered.”

He stopped a few feet from God, close enough that the last dim light of the Creator’s form flickered against the King’s boots.

“The first time you thought that I could be destroyed,” Godric said, “the weakness paradox triggered. Not when you came here today. Long before. The instant that thought formed in you, before time had a name for before, my amplification rate permanently increased. I gained perfect immunity to everything you are. I gained flawless mastery of every act you could ever commit. I could deny you the concept of your own attack with less than a thought. That was the paradox working as it always does. But here is the part that should keep you awake in the void, old man. I did not need it. I did not need the paradox, or the immune system, or the infinite backups, or anything the Stasis Event made of me. The me from Year Zero, newly woken, still clouded with the grief of Olympus, that pathetically weak version of me that I have long since outgrown without end, could have annihilated you with a sigh. Before I ever became the thing you fear, before the first day of my reign was over, you were already less than nothing beside me.”

God’s face was no longer a face. It was a white, boiling mask of pure realization. I saw His eyes widen, and the whole of His omniscience, that great seeing that had watched every life and every death and every possible path, turned inward and tried to find a future in which His attack had worked. There was none. There had never been none. There had only been the lie He told Himself in the dark behind all prayers.

“You are not my creator,” Godric said. “Not anymore. My origin is not in your hands. The Stasis Event was made by my future self, a being so far beyond me in this moment that if all of existence and all of not-existence and every version of me except him were gathered together, they would not disturb the first layer of his smallest dormant aura. He looked back across the whole of time and placed the seed of my power inside the wound you allowed to happen. You did not make me. You only lit the candle of a mortal king, and then the future of that king returned to become his own maker. You are a prefix. A preface. A piece of front matter in a story whose author sits on a throne above all stories.”

God’s light went out. Not all at once. It guttered like a torch in a rain that had no end. The beard of first snow turned to ash. The white robe that had been the fabric of all sacred law began to come apart at the seams. His hands, the hands that had shaped the first clay, trembled, and the motion itself was an impossible thing, because He had never trembled. He had never known failure.

He tried to speak. I do not think He knew what He was asking. It might have been mercy. It might have been only the last word of a creator who had just learned that creation no longer needed him.

Godric did not let the word finish. He lifted one hand, not in a blow, not in a wave. It was the smallest movement I have ever seen from him, the kind of movement a man makes when he turns a page in a book he has already read too many times. His fingers opened. Then they closed.

And God was destroyed.

I must write this part exactly as I saw it, because no one else will believe it. The destruction was not fast. It was not a light or a fire or a falling star. It was a slow, precise, almost gentle unraveling of everything God had ever been. The center of His chest, where the King’s blade had failed to cut, began to fold inward. The fold deepened, layer after layer, and each layer was a separate agony. His omnipotence was pulled through the fold first, not removed but inverted, turned against Him. The power that had set the stars spinning became a hot, grinding pressure inside His own ribs. His omniscience came next, and the knowledge of every life He had ever made was poured into Him at once, but not as memory. As pain. He felt every death, every grief, every loneliness, every sin, every scream that had ever risen from the worlds He had made, all at once, and then all again, and then again, endlessly, inside a moment that did not pass.

His wings, if wings they could be called, the vast layers of His authority that had covered the whole sky of the unseen, were peeled away. They did not fall. They were drawn into the fold, one feather at a time, and each feather was a concept of law or covenant or hope, and as it was drawn in, it became a needle. Every needle pierced Him. He could not close His eyes, because the fold had reached His face, and His eyes were the last things to go. I saw them. I will see them forever. They were wide with the look of a maker who has just learned that He is not the final word.

The whole hall did not shake with His death. The whole omniverse shook. It shook exactly once, the way a sheet shakes when it is pulled from a bed, and then it followed Him.

Everything went.

I do not mean that the lights went out. The lights did not go out, because light stopped having a definition. The omniverse, all realities, all multiverses, all timelines, all possibilities, all things that could ever exist or fail to exist, were drawn after God into the fold. I saw planets stream past like dust. I saw galaxies gather into a single bright thread. I saw the conceptual realms themselves, the houses of numbers and laws and meanings, begin to tear. The whole of what is, what was, what might have been, became a single ongoing shriek that grew thinner and thinner as it fell into the King’s closing hand. I did not fall. The King had kept me in a small envelope of his attention, and from inside that envelope I watched the universe die. The gore was not gore, because gore requires bodies, but the bodies were there, all of them, every being that had ever existed, and they were pulled into the same fold, their lives and deaths and memories pressed into a single infinite point of maximum suffering. They did not go quietly. They could not. The sound of them was the sound of an entire existence being made to remember that it had never been safe.

Then Godric’s fingers closed, and the sound stopped.

The throne room was gone. The palace was gone. Thronegate was gone. There was no light, no dark, no space, no time. There was only the King, standing in the hollow that had once been the whole of everything, and me, held in a small warm pocket at his side, and in his hand a tiny, quiet darkness where God and all creation had been.

He opened his hand. The tiny darkness was still there, no larger than a seed. Godric looked at it for a long time. Then he closed his fingers again and smiled, not the smile of a tyrant enjoying his victory, but the smile of a man who had just remembered a pleasant old tune.

“I should have known,” he said. “The very last resistance. The one that was supposed to mean something. And it couldn’t even make me feel a tickle.”

He put the seed in his pocket, and then he did something I cannot begin to describe. He restored everything. Not by a word, not by a wish. He simply allowed existence to be again. The palace returned, the world returned, every world, every universe, every timeline, every soul, all of it back as if the death had never happened. But the Creator was not among them. He was still in the seed in Godric’s pocket. The new reality was identical, but it had no God. No one remembered Him. No one had ever prayed to Him. The entire structure of creation had been rewoven by the King, and in the new weave, the old author had never existed.

And that is the deepest fear I have ever known. The restored reality is real. It is exactly what came before. But the original is still compressed in Godric’s pocket, and what we live in now is the copy he made because he wished to have a palace to walk through. We are not the first world. We are the second version of the first, and the first is in his hand, small as a seed, and he does not seem to notice the weight.

Because to him, it weighs nothing. The full mass of all existence, the full history of every soul, the full weight of God’s final failure, and Godric carried it in his pocket as if it were lint. And when he lifted it, his arm did not tremble. His fingers did not strain. Because the strength in his body, the strength that had been amplifying beyond infinity for span beyond span, no longer had a limit to compare against. The whole of the Creator’s last attack had not moved a single hair on his chest. The whole of creation had died in the fold of his hand. And in the act of closing that hand, something in him had recognized the smallness of the thing he had crushed, and his amplification had responded by increasing again, and again, and again, with no end, because there was no longer any object in the omniverse large enough to give his strength a scale.

He grew stronger from that. Not from absorbing God’s power. The Creator’s power was so far beneath him that adding it would have been less than zero. He grew stronger because his own body had registered the effortlessness of his victory and decided to close the gap between himself and his own effortlessness. The gap was infinite. The closing was infinite. The gap remained infinite. And that endless chase was his nourishment. It is still happening now. It will happen forever.

Godric turned to me after the restoration and put a warm hand on my shoulder. “You are pale, Osvald,” he said. “Let us find you some wine. I think the kitchen is still standing.”

I followed him. I could not speak. I am writing this now because I must, and because I know that someone after me may read it and need to understand what the last opposition was. It was not a war. It was not a battle. It was the Creator of all things bringing the full power of His office against the King of Thronegate, and discovering that He was not even a footnote in the story.

I do not know if I am real. I do not know if any of us are. The original creation is in Godric’s pocket. The world I walk through now is the copy he made after he put it there. But I have seen his face when he smiles at me, and I have felt his hand on my shoulder, and I am afraid. Not of death. Of the fact that even the original death of everything did not disturb a single fold of his coat.

---

Clive let the journal close. The pages settled with a sound like a breath going out. The vault was dark and very quiet, and the small lamp beside him had not moved, because even the flame had learned to hold still in this place.

He did not open another journal. He knew, without being told, that there were no more. This was the end of the archive. The next shelves were empty, not because the court wizards had stopped writing, but because there was nothing left to record. No one opposed Godric after God. No one ever would again. The last enemy had been the first cause, and the first cause had died in a moment so small that the restored universe did not remember His name.

Clive sat there for a long time, holding the warm leather in his cold hands. The old fear that had haunted every journal he had ever read had not lessened. It had simply found its final shape. Godric had not merely defeated the last opposition. He had replaced the very origin of all things. The original creation was in his pocket, and the new creation walked around it, praising a king who had not even needed to lift a hand.

Somewhere above him, in the high clean rooms of the palace, Godric was probably sitting with a cup of broth, asking after the weather, warm and easy and terrible. Clive did not move. He was afraid that if he stood, he would feel the floor remember being unmade. And worse, he was afraid that it would not remember at all.
